boundaries.futures.body: Single-stock futures in this simulation settle in cash at expiry and never deliver shares. Margin, daily mark-to-market and cash settlement all move the account cash balance.
boundaries.futures.detail: Real futures may be physically settled or cash settled; this simulation uses cash settlement to avoid stock inventory and delivery workflows.
boundaries.futures.title: Futures: cash settled, no stock delivery
boundaries.history.body: Historical prices and company samples include only fictional companies that still exist today; delisted, bankrupt or acquired names are absent.
boundaries.history.detail: Historical returns, factor backtests and “buy and hold” results can therefore be overstated. Real research needs delisted companies and survivorship-bias adjustments.
boundaries.history.title: Historical data: survivorship bias is present
boundaries.intro: Accounting and risk logic are built to be verifiable, but the simulation still simplifies. Understanding the boundaries matters more than memorising conclusions.
boundaries.note: These boundaries apply across stocks, ETFs, options, futures, history scenarios and challenge mode.
boundaries.options.body: Options deliver shares at the strike at expiry or on exercise; when cash or shares are insufficient the payoff falls back to intrinsic-value cash settlement.
boundaries.options.detail: American mode assigns deep in-the-money short legs deterministically; counterparty behaviour, borrow costs and dividend adjustments remain outside this simulation.
boundaries.options.title: Options: European / American and physical delivery
boundaries.subtitle: This game is a teaching simulation, not an exchange. The boundaries below are stated explicitly instead of hidden.
boundaries.title: Real-data and matching boundaries

demo.allocation.desc: Adjust stock and bond weights to see the allocation, expected return and volatility.
demo.allocation.note: Assumes stocks 7% / 16% volatility, bonds 3.5% / 6%, cash 1.5% / 0.5%. Correlations are ignored, so actual portfolio volatility can differ.
demo.allocation.title: Asset Allocation Lab
demo.candle.desc: Judge each candle as bullish or bearish; three correct answers complete the practice.
demo.candle.note: High and low are adjusted to cover open and close so impossible candles cannot be drawn.
demo.candle.title: Candle Anatomy Lab
demo.common.note: This is a teaching demo with its own parameters. It never changes your simulated account, positions or orders.
demo.compounding.desc: Adjust starting capital, monthly contributions, annual return and years to see the compounding curve and final value.
demo.compounding.note: Assumes contributions at month-end, a constant return and monthly compounding. Taxes, inflation and volatility are excluded.
demo.compounding.title: Compounding Calculator
demo.dcf.desc: Adjust cash flow, growth, discount and terminal assumptions to calculate intrinsic value.
demo.dcf.invalid: Current assumptions are invalid: the discount rate must exceed perpetual growth, and cash flow and shares must be positive.
demo.dcf.note: This is a transparent teaching model that ignores taxes, working-capital changes and scenario probabilities. Not investment advice.
demo.dcf.title: DCF Valuation Lab
demo.diversification.desc: Compare the annualised volatility of one stock with an equal-weight basket of three companies from different sectors.
demo.diversification.note: Volatility uses the last 60 daily returns, annualised. Past volatility is not a forecast, and a basket does not guarantee lower risk.
demo.diversification.title: Diversification Lab
demo.dividend.desc: Change shares, price and yield to see annual income and the effect of ten years of reinvestment.
demo.dividend.note: Reinvestment assumes dividends buy more shares at the same price each year and a constant yield. Taxes and price changes are excluded.
demo.dividend.tenYear: Annual income after 10 years of reinvestment
demo.dividend.title: Dividend Cash-Flow Lab
demo.financials.desc: Open any company's income statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement on the trade page.
demo.financials.note: Figures are generated from company fundamentals and keep assets = liabilities + equity, but are simplified teaching simulations. Units are millions of USD.
demo.financials.title: Financial Statements Walkthrough
demo.futuresPnl.desc: Choose direction, entry and settlement prices to see notional, margin and P&L.
demo.futuresPnl.note: Excludes fees and slippage; losses can exceed margin.
demo.futuresPnl.title: Futures P&L lab
demo.greeks.desc: Adjust spot, strike, volatility and time to expiry to see the premium and all five Greeks.
demo.greeks.note: Estimated with a 4% risk-free rate and Black-Scholes; teaching only.
demo.greeks.title: Greeks lab
demo.hedge.desc: Adjust shares, stock price, hedge ratio and futures price to see contracts needed and residual exposure.
demo.hedge.note: Simplified model assuming futures and spot move together; real hedges carry basis and correlation risk.
demo.hedge.title: Hedge-ratio lab
demo.indicators.death: SMA20 is below SMA50: the short-term trend is weaker.
demo.indicators.desc: Compare SMA 5 with SMA 10 and decide which average is smoother.
demo.indicators.golden: SMA20 is above SMA50: the short-term trend is stronger.
demo.indicators.notEnough: Not enough history to compute the long moving average yet.
demo.indicators.note: Blue is SMA20 and orange is SMA50. Indicators use only current and past data.
demo.indicators.title: Moving-Average Smoothness Lab
demo.lab.candle.prompt: Read this candle: did it close above or below the open? Get three right in a row.
demo.lab.candle.wrong: Check the body direction: green/up means close above open.
demo.lab.dcf.error: Discount rate must exceed terminal growth.
demo.lab.dcf.prompt: Adjust the assumptions and discount projected cash flows.
demo.lab.indicators.prompt: Here are 12 daily closes. Switch between SMA 5 and SMA 10 and compare smoothness.
demo.lab.indicators.question: Which average is smoother?
demo.lab.indicators.viewBoth: View both SMA 5 and SMA 10 first.
demo.lab.indicators.wrong: Longer periods smooth more; compare again.
demo.lab.note: Progress is recorded only after a real interaction.
demo.limitOrder.desc: Set a limit and simulate a price path over time to see whether the order would fill.
demo.limitOrder.filled: The price touched your limit at step {tick}, filling the order at {price}.
demo.limitOrder.hint: The path uses its own random numbers and is unrelated to your real account.
demo.limitOrder.idle: Set a limit and run the simulation to watch the path and result.
demo.limitOrder.notFilled: The price never reached your limit within {ticks} steps, so the order stayed unfilled.
demo.limitOrder.title: Limit Order Fill Simulator
demo.macro.desc: Adjust policy rate, inflation and growth to see the real rate, cycle regime and a sample discount rate.
demo.macro.note: A simplified macro teaching model. The numbers do not represent any real economy and are not a forecast.
demo.macro.title: Macro Scenario Lab
demo.margin.desc: Adjust cash, price and shares to see the loan, equity, leverage and daily interest.
demo.margin.note: Uses an 8% annual rate and 252 trading days; excludes commissions and slippage.
demo.margin.title: Margin and leverage lab
demo.marketCap.desc: Drag the share price to see how one company's market cap changes, and compare it with the others.
demo.marketCap.title: Share Price and Market Cap Lab
demo.optionPayoff.desc: Switch between calls and puts, adjust strike, premium and expiry price, and watch the payoff and breakeven.
demo.optionPayoff.note: Excludes commissions and taxes; European options settle only at expiry.
demo.optionPayoff.title: Option payoff lab
demo.orderBook.desc: Build a five-level book from the current quote and watch a large order consume depth and slip.
demo.orderBook.note: The teaching book is derived from the quote, not real orders; real depth changes quickly.
demo.orderBook.title: Order book and slippage lab
demo.pnl.chartNote: The x-axis spans the sell price range; the y-axis is net P&L.
demo.pnl.desc: Adjust the buy price, sell price and quantity to see net P&L and return change.
demo.pnl.title: Profit and Loss Calculator
demo.risk.desc: Use account risk and stop distance to calculate shares, position value and exposure.
demo.risk.note: Ignores commissions, slippage and gaps; a stop price does not guarantee a fill.
demo.risk.title: Position Sizing Lab
demo.shortPnl.desc: Adjust the sale price, cover price and share count to see short P&L, return and collateral.
demo.shortPnl.note: Excludes borrow fees, commissions and dividends; short losses can exceed the collateral.
demo.shortPnl.title: Short P&L lab
demo.spread.desc: Change the quantity and see how the gap between the bid and ask becomes a real cost.
demo.spread.hint: The gap between what buyers offer and sellers ask is the spread.
demo.spread.title: Bid/Ask Spread Lab
demo.stockStyle.desc: Pick a company to see its style label, sector and dividend yield, and compare what each style means.
demo.stockStyle.title: Stock Style Explorer
demo.stopOrder.desc: Compare the distance, risk and locked gain of a fixed stop and a trailing stop.
demo.stopOrder.note: Excludes slippage and gaps; the stop price does not guarantee a fill.
demo.stopOrder.title: Stop and trailing-stop lab
demo.strategies.desc: Compare equal-weight style baskets over different lookback windows using the simulated market history.
demo.strategies.note: Simulated equal-weight history, not a real backtest, and not a forecast of future returns.
demo.strategies.synthetic: Fewer than 90 simulated sessions are available, so a teaching synthetic series is shown.
demo.strategies.title: Style Strategy Comparison
demo.strategyPayoff.desc: Choose covered call, CSP, vertical spreads, straddles or strangles and inspect payoff, max loss and max profit.
demo.strategyPayoff.note: Fees and taxes excluded; straddles and strangles have theoretically unlimited profit but need a large move.
demo.strategyPayoff.title: Option strategy payoff lab
demo.strategyPayoff.unavailable: The current chain cannot build that strategy.
demo.stressTest.desc: Adjust equity, leverage and shock size to see the loss and whether the account survives.
demo.stressTest.note: Simplified stress test assuming all positions fall together; liquidity and slippage excluded.
demo.stressTest.title: Stress-test lab

glossary.subtitle: Understand terms in Chinese and English. {count} foundational concepts included.
glossary.terms.adverseSelection.def: Information asymmetry makes market makers more likely to trade with informed counterparties.
glossary.terms.adverseSelection.example: The price rises right after a maker buys, eroding spread income.
glossary.terms.adverseSelection.name: Adverse selection
glossary.terms.ask.def: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept. Buys usually execute at the ask.
glossary.terms.ask.example: An ask of $50.02 means someone is willing to sell at that price.
glossary.terms.ask.name: Ask
glossary.terms.assetAllocation.def: The process of dividing money across asset classes and weights, shaping a portfolio's risk and return.
glossary.terms.assetAllocation.example: A 60% stock / 40% bond portfolio is usually steadier than an all-stock portfolio.
glossary.terms.assetAllocation.name: Asset allocation
glossary.terms.assignment.def: When an in-the-money option expires, the seller is obligated to perform under the contract.
glossary.terms.assignment.example: A short $50 call with the stock at $60 must deliver at $50 or cash-settle.
glossary.terms.assignment.name: Assignment
glossary.terms.attribution.def: An analysis that decomposes portfolio return into allocation, selection, interaction and fee sources.
glossary.terms.attribution.example: The portfolio beats its benchmark by 2%, with 1.2% attributed to a technology overweight.
glossary.terms.attribution.name: Performance attribution
glossary.terms.balanceSheet.def: A snapshot of assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity; the identity is assets = liabilities + equity.
glossary.terms.balanceSheet.name: Balance sheet
glossary.terms.basis.def: The futures price minus spot, usually reflecting carry and converging toward expiry.
glossary.terms.basis.example: Spot $50 and futures $50.33 give a $0.33 basis.
glossary.terms.basis.name: Basis
glossary.terms.bid.def: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay. Sells usually execute at the bid.
glossary.terms.bid.example: A bid of $49.98 means someone is willing to buy at that price.
glossary.terms.bid.name: Bid
glossary.terms.broker.def: A financial firm or platform that accepts investor orders and sends them to an exchange for execution. Brokers charge commissions.
glossary.terms.broker.example: The order ticket in this game plays the role of a broker.
glossary.terms.broker.name: Broker
glossary.terms.callOption.def: The right to buy the underlying at the strike on expiry; a bullish expression.
glossary.terms.callOption.example: A $50 call has $10 of intrinsic value when the stock reaches $60.
glossary.terms.callOption.name: Call option
glossary.terms.candle.def: A chart shape built from one period's open, high, low and close; the body connects open and close while wicks reach the high and low.
glossary.terms.candle.example: Open $48, high $52, low $46.5, close $51.2 forms a bullish candle.
glossary.terms.candle.name: Candlestick
glossary.terms.carryTrade.def: Borrowing in a low-yield currency and investing in a high-yield currency to earn the rate differential.
glossary.terms.carryTrade.example: Borrowing at 1% to invest at 5% implies 4% carry, but currency depreciation can wipe it out.
glossary.terms.carryTrade.name: Carry trade
glossary.terms.cashSecuredPut.def: Selling a put while reserving strike × 100 in cash, accepting a possible purchase at the strike.
glossary.terms.cashSecuredPut.example: Sell a $45 put for $1.20 and reserve $4,500.
glossary.terms.cashSecuredPut.name: Cash-secured put
glossary.terms.commission.def: A fee charged by a broker for executing a trade. Commissions directly reduce net profit.
glossary.terms.commission.example: This game charges a flat $1.00 commission per fill.
glossary.terms.commission.name: Commission
glossary.terms.compounding.def: Reinvesting interest or returns so that future periods earn a return on them too. The effect grows with time.
glossary.terms.compounding.example: $1,000 at 8% compounded annually is about $2,158.92 after 10 years.
glossary.terms.compounding.name: Compounding
glossary.terms.comps.def: Pricing a target using valuation multiples from similar companies.
glossary.terms.comps.example: A peer average P/E of 18 and target EPS of 2 imply about 36 per share.
glossary.terms.comps.name: Comparable company analysis
glossary.terms.costBasis.def: The total amount paid for a position, including the purchase price and buy fees. Average cost = cost basis ÷ shares held.
glossary.terms.costBasis.example: Buying 20 shares at $50 with a $1 commission gives a $1,001 cost basis.
glossary.terms.costBasis.name: Cost basis
glossary.terms.coveredCall.def: Holding 100 shares and selling one call; the stock covers delivery in exchange for premium.
glossary.terms.coveredCall.example: Hold $50 stock and sell a $55 call for $1.50.
glossary.terms.coveredCall.name: Covered call
glossary.terms.cyclicalStock.def: A stock whose earnings swing with the economic cycle, common in industrials, materials, energy and discretionary consumer sectors.
glossary.terms.cyclicalStock.example: Orders and profits rise in expansions and can fall sharply in recessions.
glossary.terms.cyclicalStock.name: Cyclical stock
glossary.terms.dcf.def: Valuation that discounts future free cash flow at a risk-adjusted rate and adds a terminal value to estimate enterprise value.
glossary.terms.dcf.example: Next-year FCF of $100M at a 10% discount rate is worth about $90.91M today.
glossary.terms.dcf.name: Discounted cash flow (DCF)
glossary.terms.deltaHedge.def: Using the underlying to offset an option book’s Delta exposure, making it temporarily neutral to small price moves.
glossary.terms.deltaHedge.example: A book with 500 shares of Delta is temporarily neutral after shorting 500 shares.
glossary.terms.deltaHedge.name: Delta hedging
glossary.terms.dilution.def: Issuing new shares reduces existing shareholders’ ownership percentage.
glossary.terms.dilution.example: A 20% share issuance dilutes existing owners’ stakes.
glossary.terms.dilution.name: Dilution
glossary.terms.diversification.def: Spreading money across different assets to reduce company- or sector-specific risk. It cannot remove overall market risk.
glossary.terms.diversification.example: Spreading money equally across three sectors softens the impact of one company failing.
glossary.terms.diversification.name: Diversification
glossary.terms.dividend.def: Cash a company distributes to shareholders from profits. It is not guaranteed: the payout can be cut, suspended or cancelled.
glossary.terms.dividend.example: You hold 100 shares with a $0.60 dividend per share, so you receive $60 in cash.
glossary.terms.dividend.name: Dividend
glossary.terms.dividendYield.def: Annual dividend per share ÷ current share price × 100%. A falling price raises the yield, but that does not make the company stronger.
glossary.terms.dividendYield.example: Annual dividend $1.20 per share and a $40.00 price give a yield of 3.00%.
glossary.terms.dividendYield.name: Dividend yield
glossary.terms.drawdown.def: The fall in equity from a previous peak; large drawdowns significantly slow compounding.
glossary.terms.drawdown.example: Falling from $10,000 to $6,000 is a 40% drawdown.
glossary.terms.drawdown.name: Drawdown
glossary.terms.etf.def: A basket of assets traded on an exchange like a stock, usually tracking an index, sector or theme.
glossary.terms.etf.example: One broad-market ETF share gives exposure to all of its underlying holdings.
glossary.terms.etf.name: ETF
glossary.terms.exDividendDate.def: Buyers on or after this date normally do not receive the declared dividend, and the share price adjusts down by roughly the dividend.
glossary.terms.exDividendDate.example: Hold 200 shares paying $0.50 each before the ex-date to receive $100; the price moves from about $25.00 to $24.50.
glossary.terms.exDividendDate.name: Ex-dividend date
glossary.terms.exchange.def: An organised marketplace that matches buy and sell orders, publishes prices and sets trading rules. The exchange itself does not trade shares.
glossary.terms.exchange.example: All fictional company orders in this game match on the simulated exchange.
glossary.terms.exchange.name: Stock exchange
glossary.terms.factorModel.def: A model that explains asset returns with common factors such as market, industry and style.
glossary.terms.factorModel.example: A portfolio with 0.8 value exposure benefits when value rebounds.
glossary.terms.factorModel.name: Factor model
glossary.terms.freeCashFlow.def: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure; cash available for dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
glossary.terms.freeCashFlow.example: Operating cash flow $300M minus capex $80M gives free cash flow of $220M.
glossary.terms.freeCashFlow.name: Free cash flow
glossary.terms.futuresContract.def: An agreement to trade the underlying at a fixed price on a future date, requiring margin and P&L on full notional.
glossary.terms.futuresContract.example: One $50 future has $5,000 notional and about $750 margin.
glossary.terms.futuresContract.name: Futures contract
glossary.terms.gammaScalping.def: Buying options and dynamically delta hedging to profit when realised volatility exceeds implied volatility.
glossary.terms.gammaScalping.example: When realised volatility exceeds IV, repeated hedge adjustments can cover the option cost.
glossary.terms.gammaScalping.name: Gamma scalping
glossary.terms.gdp.def: The total output of an economy over a period, used to measure economic growth.
glossary.terms.gdp.example: GDP growing 3% year over year usually means an expanding economy.
glossary.terms.gdp.name: Gross domestic product (GDP)
glossary.terms.greeks.def: Sensitivities of option prices to different inputs: Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega and Rho.
glossary.terms.greeks.example: A delta of 0.5 means the premium rises about $0.50 for a $1 move.
glossary.terms.greeks.name: Greeks
glossary.terms.growthStock.def: A company growing revenue and earnings faster than the market, usually reinvesting profits, paying little or no dividend, with higher valuation and volatility.
glossary.terms.growthStock.example: A company growing revenue 25% a year may earn a high P/E, but the price can fall sharply when growth slows.
glossary.terms.growthStock.name: Growth stock
glossary.terms.hedge.def: An offsetting position that lowers directional risk but leaves basis, correlation and margin risk.
glossary.terms.hedge.example: Hold $50,000 of stock and short an equivalent futures notional.
glossary.terms.hedge.name: Hedge
glossary.terms.impliedVolatility.def: The market’s price for future movement; higher implied volatility makes options more expensive.
glossary.terms.impliedVolatility.example: When implied volatility rises from 30% to 40%, call and put premiums usually rise.
glossary.terms.impliedVolatility.name: Implied volatility
glossary.terms.incomeStatement.def: A report starting with revenue, subtracting costs and expenses and ending with net income; margins measure profitability.
glossary.terms.incomeStatement.example: Revenue $1,000M, gross profit $520M and net income $200M gives a 20% net margin.
glossary.terms.incomeStatement.name: Income statement
glossary.terms.inflation.def: A broad and sustained rise in prices, which reduces the purchasing power of cash and fixed income.
glossary.terms.inflation.example: At 4% inflation, goods costing 100 today may cost about 104 next year.
glossary.terms.inflation.name: Inflation
glossary.terms.interestRate.def: The cost of money. Higher rates raise discount rates and funding costs, usually lowering asset valuations.
glossary.terms.interestRate.example: A discount rate rising from 8% to 10% lowers the present value of future cash flow.
glossary.terms.interestRate.name: Interest rate
glossary.terms.ipo.def: A company’s first public share sale and listing.
glossary.terms.ipo.example: Priced at 30 and closing at 36 on day one is a 20% first-day premium.
glossary.terms.ipo.name: Initial public offering (IPO)
glossary.terms.limitOrder.def: An order that sets a maximum purchase price or minimum sale price. It fills only at that price or better.
glossary.terms.limitOrder.example: With the market at $50, a buy limit at $48 fills only if the price falls to $48 or lower.
glossary.terms.limitOrder.name: Limit order
glossary.terms.liquidity.def: How easily a stock trades and how close fills are to the expected price. Liquid stocks have tight spreads and fast execution.
glossary.terms.liquidity.example: A heavily traded large cap is usually more liquid than an obscure small cap.
glossary.terms.liquidity.name: Liquidity
glossary.terms.lookAheadBias.def: Using information that was not available at the time in a backtest, inflating results.
glossary.terms.lookAheadBias.example: Generating today’s signal from the next 20 days of returns cannot be traded live.
glossary.terms.lookAheadBias.name: Look-ahead bias
glossary.terms.margin.def: The equity that must be posted to cover potential losses on borrowed cash or securities.
glossary.terms.margin.example: Buy $15,000 of stock with $10,000 of your own cash; the margin ratio is 2/3.
glossary.terms.margin.name: Margin
glossary.terms.marginCall.def: A broker demand to add funds or face forced liquidation when equity falls below maintenance.
glossary.terms.marginCall.example: A price drop pushes equity below maintenance and the account is liquidated.
glossary.terms.marginCall.name: Margin call
glossary.terms.marketCap.def: The total market value of a company, equal to share price times shares outstanding. It reflects overall company size, not the price of one share.
glossary.terms.marketCap.example: $42.50 × 180 million shares = about $7.65 billion market cap.
glossary.terms.marketCap.name: Market capitalisation
glossary.terms.marketMaker.def: A firm that continuously quotes bid and ask prices to provide liquidity.
glossary.terms.marketMaker.example: After buying 10,000 shares, a long-inventory maker lowers the bid to encourage selling.
glossary.terms.marketMaker.name: Market maker
glossary.terms.marketOrder.def: An order to trade immediately at the best available price. It prioritises execution speed over price certainty.
glossary.terms.marketOrder.example: A market buy of 10 shares fills at the current ask.
glossary.terms.marketOrder.name: Market order
glossary.terms.momentum.def: The tendency of recent price trends to persist; momentum strategies buy strength and sell weakness.
glossary.terms.momentum.example: A stock that outperformed over three months may stay in a momentum portfolio.
glossary.terms.momentum.name: Momentum
glossary.terms.nav.def: Fund assets minus liabilities divided by fund shares, showing what one fund share is worth.
glossary.terms.nav.example: Assets 120m, liabilities 10m and 10m shares give NAV = 11.
glossary.terms.nav.name: Net asset value (NAV)
glossary.terms.optionContract.def: Gives the buyer the right to buy or sell the underlying at the strike on expiry, in exchange for a premium.
glossary.terms.optionContract.example: An AURA $55 call with 30 days left costs $1.20.
glossary.terms.optionContract.name: Option contract
glossary.terms.optionPremium.def: The price paid for the option, equal to intrinsic value plus time value.
glossary.terms.optionPremium.example: $2 intrinsic plus $1.10 time value gives a $3.10 premium.
glossary.terms.optionPremium.name: Option premium
glossary.terms.orderBook.def: The list of resting bids and asks by price, showing size at each level.
glossary.terms.orderBook.example: Bid $49.99 and ask $50.01 give a $0.02 spread.
glossary.terms.orderBook.name: Order book
glossary.terms.overfitting.def: A model fits noise in the training data and performs much worse out of sample.
glossary.terms.overfitting.example: A 90% training accuracy and 52% out-of-sample accuracy means the model memorised noise.
glossary.terms.overfitting.name: Overfitting
glossary.terms.payoutRatio.def: Dividend per share ÷ earnings per share. It shows how much profit is distributed rather than retained for reinvestment.
glossary.terms.payoutRatio.example: EPS of $2.00 with a $1.00 annual dividend gives a 50% payout ratio.
glossary.terms.payoutRatio.name: Payout ratio
glossary.terms.positionSizing.def: Calculating position size from acceptable risk and stop distance rather than buying on impulse.
glossary.terms.positionSizing.example: A $10,000 account risking 1% with $4 risk per share buys 25 shares.
glossary.terms.positionSizing.name: Position sizing
glossary.terms.priceImpact.def: A large order consumes order-book depth and moves the price.
glossary.terms.priceImpact.example: Buying more than the best-level depth worsens the average fill.
glossary.terms.priceImpact.name: Price impact
glossary.terms.putOption.def: The right to sell the underlying at the strike on expiry; used for bearish views or hedging.
glossary.terms.putOption.example: A $50 put has $10 of intrinsic value when the stock falls to $40.
glossary.terms.putOption.name: Put option
glossary.terms.realizedPnl.def: The gain or loss locked in after selling, equal to net sale proceeds minus the matching cost basis.
glossary.terms.realizedPnl.example: Net sale proceeds $1,099 against a $1,001 cost basis: realized gain of $98.
glossary.terms.realizedPnl.name: Realized P&L
glossary.terms.returnRate.def: P&L expressed as a percentage of the capital invested, allowing comparison across different position sizes.
glossary.terms.returnRate.example: Invest $1,001 and gain $98: a return of about 9.79%.
glossary.terms.returnRate.name: Return
glossary.terms.riskBudget.def: A method that allocates total portfolio risk across assets or strategies, focusing on risk contribution rather than capital weight alone.
glossary.terms.riskBudget.example: Two strategies each hold 50% of capital but one contributes 80% of volatility; risk budgeting cuts its weight.
glossary.terms.riskBudget.name: Risk budget
glossary.terms.rsi.def: A momentum indicator comparing recent gains and losses on a 0–100 scale, with common thresholds of 70 and 30.
glossary.terms.rsi.example: RSI above 70 shows strong momentum and possible overbought conditions, but does not guarantee a fall.
glossary.terms.rsi.name: Relative Strength Index (RSI)
glossary.terms.sharePrice.def: The current market price of one share, continually updated by quotes and trades.
glossary.terms.sharePrice.example: A last price of $42.50 means the most recent trade happened at that price.
glossary.terms.sharePrice.name: Share price
glossary.terms.shareholder.def: A person or institution that owns shares in a company. Shareholders typically have voting rights, dividend rights and the right to transfer their shares.
glossary.terms.shareholder.example: When you buy AURA, you become one of Auralis Robotics' shareholders.
glossary.terms.shareholder.name: Shareholder
glossary.terms.sharpeRatio.def: Excess return divided by volatility, measuring reward per unit of risk.
glossary.terms.sharpeRatio.example: With 12% return, 3% risk-free rate and 18% volatility, Sharpe = 0.5.
glossary.terms.sharpeRatio.name: Sharpe ratio
glossary.terms.shortSelling.def: Borrowing shares to sell them now, aiming to buy them back cheaper and profit from the difference.
glossary.terms.shortSelling.example: Short at $50 and cover at $40 for a $10 per-share gross profit.
glossary.terms.shortSelling.name: Short selling
glossary.terms.slippage.def: The difference between the expected price at order entry and the actual fill. It is more visible in volatile or illiquid markets.
glossary.terms.slippage.example: You see $50.00 but fill at $50.40; the extra $0.40 is slippage.
glossary.terms.slippage.name: Slippage
glossary.terms.sma.def: The arithmetic average of the last N closes, used to smooth noise and observe trend.
glossary.terms.sma.name: Simple moving average (SMA)
glossary.terms.spread.def: The difference between the ask and the bid. It is an implicit trading cost and is usually wider for less liquid stocks.
glossary.terms.spread.example: Bid $49.98 and ask $50.02 means a $0.04 spread.
glossary.terms.spread.name: Bid/ask spread
glossary.terms.stock.def: A tradable certificate representing a share of ownership in a company. Holding stock makes you a shareholder with a proportional claim on profits and residual assets.
glossary.terms.stock.example: A company issues one million shares. Owning 1,000 shares gives you 0.1% ownership.
glossary.terms.stock.name: Stock
glossary.terms.stopOrder.def: An order that becomes a market order once the trigger price is reached, used to cap losses.
glossary.terms.stopOrder.example: Buy at $100 with a $92 sell stop; a break below sells at market.
glossary.terms.stopOrder.name: Stop order
glossary.terms.straddle.def: Buying a call and a put at the same strike and expiry; a bet on large movement rather than direction.
glossary.terms.straddle.example: A $50 straddle costs $400 with breakevens at $46 and $54.
glossary.terms.straddle.name: Straddle
glossary.terms.strangle.def: Buying out-of-the-money calls and puts at different strikes for less premium but needing a larger move.
glossary.terms.strangle.example: A $55 call and $45 put cost $200 with breakevens at $44 and $56.
glossary.terms.strangle.name: Strangle
glossary.terms.strikePrice.def: The contracted price at which the underlying can be bought or sold; it sets intrinsic value.
glossary.terms.strikePrice.example: A $50 call with spot at $55 has $5 of intrinsic value.
glossary.terms.strikePrice.name: Strike price
glossary.terms.systemicRisk.def: Risk that spreads through leverage, liquidity and counterparty chains across the market.
glossary.terms.systemicRisk.example: Forced selling pushes prices down and triggers more liquidation and liquidity stress.
glossary.terms.systemicRisk.name: Systemic risk
glossary.terms.ticker.def: A short code used by an exchange to identify a listed company, usually one to five letters.
glossary.terms.ticker.example: AURA is the ticker for Auralis Robotics in this game.
glossary.terms.ticker.name: Ticker symbol
glossary.terms.trailingStop.def: A stop that tightens as the price moves favourably and never loosens.
glossary.terms.trailingStop.example: Buy at $100 with a $6 trail; after $120 the stop moves to $114.
glossary.terms.trailingStop.name: Trailing stop
glossary.terms.unrealizedPnl.def: The floating gain or loss on a position you still hold, equal to current market value minus cost basis. It moves with the price.
glossary.terms.unrealizedPnl.example: Cost basis $1,001, current value $1,100: unrealized gain of $99.
glossary.terms.unrealizedPnl.name: Unrealized P&L
glossary.terms.valueStock.def: A stock priced low relative to earnings, assets or cash flow. It may be undervalued, or cheap because fundamentals are weakening.
glossary.terms.valueStock.example: A P/E of 10 may look cheap, but you still need to check whether earnings are stable.
glossary.terms.valueStock.name: Value stock
glossary.terms.verticalSpread.def: A long and a short option with the same expiry and different strikes, expressing direction with defined risk.
glossary.terms.verticalSpread.example: Buy the $50 call and sell the $55 call for a $2 net debit.
glossary.terms.verticalSpread.name: Vertical spread
glossary.terms.volatilitySmile.def: Implied volatility differs by strike, often forming a smile or skew.
glossary.terms.volatilitySmile.example: Low-strike puts show higher IV than at-the-money options, producing a downward slope.
glossary.terms.volatilitySmile.name: Volatility smile
glossary.terms.wacc.def: The weighted average cost of equity and debt capital, commonly used as the DCF discount rate.
glossary.terms.wacc.example: With 12% equity cost, 5% debt cost and 50/50 weights, after-tax WACC is about 8.5%.
glossary.terms.wacc.name: WACC
glossary.terms.yieldCurve.def: The relationship between government bond yields across maturities.
glossary.terms.yieldCurve.example: Two-year 4.5% and ten-year 3.8% is an inverted curve.
glossary.terms.yieldCurve.name: Yield curve

history.events.2008.e1.text: BNP Paribas froze three funds and global markets began repricing subprime mortgage risk.
history.events.2008.e1.title: Subprime stress surfaces
history.events.2008.e10.text: The Fed announced large purchases of mortgage-backed securities; the policy pivot became a major support.
history.events.2008.e10.title: Quantitative easing begins
history.events.2008.e11.text: Amid extreme pessimism, major indices hit their crisis lows and began to recover.
history.events.2008.e11.title: The market bottom
history.events.2008.e12.text: Economic data showed signs of stabilisation and markets rebounded from the bottom, though jobs and credit remained weak.
history.events.2008.e12.title: Recovery hopes build
history.events.2008.e2.text: The Federal Reserve cut rates by 50 basis points. Markets bounced briefly, but credit problems persisted.
history.events.2008.e2.title: The Fed starts cutting
history.events.2008.e3.text: The Nasdaq Composite peaked in autumn 2007 and then entered a long decline.
history.events.2008.e3.title: Nasdaq peaks
history.events.2008.e4.text: With Fed support, JPMorgan acquired Bear Stearns, turning investment-bank risk into a systemic event.
history.events.2008.e4.title: Bear Stearns rescue
history.events.2008.e5.text: The US Treasury pledged support for the two mortgage giants and markets stabilised briefly.
history.events.2008.e5.title: Fannie and Freddie backstop
history.events.2008.e6.text: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, one of the largest corporate failures in US history, freezing global credit.
history.events.2008.e6.title: Lehman Brothers fails
history.events.2008.e7.text: The US government provided an emergency loan to AIG as fear spread from banks to insurers and the financial system.
history.events.2008.e7.title: AIG is rescued
history.events.2008.e8.text: The House rejected the bailout plan and the Dow fell about 777 points in a single session.
history.events.2008.e8.title: TARP vote fails
history.events.2008.e9.text: The rescue plan passed, but markets still had to digest recession and deleveraging pressure.
history.events.2008.e9.title: TARP signed into law
history.events.2015.e1.text: A renminbi devaluation and China growth fears triggered a global selloff and violent Nasdaq swings.
history.events.2015.e1.title: Global risk-off selloff
history.events.2015.e10.text: Rapid hikes exposed bank asset-liability mismatches; SVB was taken over and contagion fears spread.
history.events.2015.e10.title: Silicon Valley Bank fails
history.events.2015.e11.text: A stronger yen triggered an unwinding of carry trades and a sharp but brief global selloff.
history.events.2015.e11.title: Yen carry unwind
history.events.2015.e12.text: A low-cost AI model forced a repricing of compute demand and whipsawed chip and technology shares.
history.events.2015.e12.title: AI competition shock
history.events.2015.e2.text: The UK voted to leave the EU, sparking a global flight to safety and a technology selloff.
history.events.2015.e2.title: Brexit referendum
history.events.2015.e3.text: Crowded low-volatility trades unwound, the VIX surged and major indices fell sharply.
history.events.2015.e3.title: Volatility spike
history.events.2015.e4.text: Rate-hike expectations and growth fears combined to knock markets down before Christmas.
history.events.2015.e4.title: Year-end growth scare
history.events.2015.e5.text: COVID-19 spread globally and markets entered a rapid decline.
history.events.2015.e5.title: Pandemic shock begins
history.events.2015.e6.text: With Fed and fiscal support expectations, the Nasdaq hit a cycle low and began a historic rebound.
history.events.2015.e6.title: Pandemic bottom
history.events.2015.e7.text: Low rates and stay-at-home demand drove record technology gains; the Nasdaq peaked in late 2021.
history.events.2015.e7.title: Tech peaks
history.events.2015.e8.text: The Fed began raising rates and growth-stock valuations came under pressure.
history.events.2015.e8.title: Hiking cycle starts
history.events.2015.e9.text: Inflation and rate hikes drove a deep technology drawdown.
history.events.2015.e9.title: 2022 low
history.events.2020.e1.text: Markets entered the pandemic at record highs, dominated by low volatility and optimism.
history.events.2020.e1.title: The year opens at highs
history.events.2020.e10.text: Vaccine efficacy data triggered a rotation from technology into cyclicals.
history.events.2020.e10.title: Vaccine breakthrough
history.events.2020.e11.text: The Nasdaq finished the year sharply higher as the pandemic became a tech catalyst.
history.events.2020.e11.title: 2020 closes
history.events.2020.e2.text: COVID-19 spread globally and risk assets began a rapid decline.
history.events.2020.e2.title: Pandemic shock begins
history.events.2020.e3.text: Falling oil and pandemic fears triggered a 15-minute market halt.
history.events.2020.e3.title: First circuit breaker
history.events.2020.e4.text: WHO declared a pandemic and travel restrictions spread; markets halted again.
history.events.2020.e4.title: Second circuit breaker
history.events.2020.e5.text: The Fed cut rates to zero and restarted asset purchases; futures still swung violently.
history.events.2020.e5.title: Emergency cut to zero
history.events.2020.e6.text: The Fed announced unlimited QE and major indices bottomed in extreme fear.
history.events.2020.e6.title: Pandemic bottom
history.events.2020.e7.text: Virus curves showed signs of flattening and technology led a market rebound.
history.events.2020.e7.title: Rebound begins
history.events.2020.e8.text: The Nasdaq erased its 2020 decline and set a new high.
history.events.2020.e8.title: Nasdaq recovers all losses
history.events.2020.e9.text: Remote-work and digital demand pushed mega-cap technology higher.
history.events.2020.e9.title: Tech accelerates
history.events.2022.e1.text: Growth stocks were valued for a low-rate world and highly sensitive to rates.
history.events.2022.e1.title: Year opens at highs
history.events.2022.e10.text: Growth stocks reached their bear-market low near year end.
history.events.2022.e10.title: Year-end low
history.events.2022.e11.text: The Nasdaq fell sharply for the year as both valuations and earnings expectations were cut.
history.events.2022.e11.title: 2022 closes
history.events.2022.e2.title: The Fed turns hawkish
history.events.2022.e3.text: The Fed raised rates by 25bp, starting the tightening cycle.
history.events.2022.e3.title: First hike
history.events.2022.e4.title: A 50bp hike
history.events.2022.e5.text: Inflation surprised to the upside and the Fed hiked 75bp.
history.events.2022.e5.title: A 75bp hike
history.events.2022.e6.text: Tightening continued and technology valuations compressed further.
history.events.2022.e6.title: Another 75bp
history.events.2022.e7.text: A hot CPI print triggered a selloff, then a violent intraday reversal.
history.events.2022.e7.title: CPI reversal
history.events.2022.e8.text: CPI came in below expectations, lifting hopes of slower tightening and tech rallied.
history.events.2022.e8.title: Inflation cools
history.events.2022.e9.text: The Fed reduced the pace to 50bp.
history.events.2022.e9.title: Hikes slow

history.scenario.2008.desc: Start on the eve of the crisis and live through the subprime shock, Lehman's collapse, TARP and the 2009 bottom using real Nasdaq daily bars.
history.scenario.2008.subtitle: Lehman, bailouts and the bottom
history.scenario.2008.tip1: Leverage and liquidity contract together in a crisis, so drawdowns dwarf normal volatility.
history.scenario.2008.tip2: Correlations rise in a crisis, so diversification can temporarily fail.
history.scenario.2008.tip3: Policy pivots often precede the bottom, but nobody can pick it precisely.
history.scenario.2008.title: 2008 Financial Crisis
history.scenario.2015.desc: Replay real US stocks from 2015 onward across technology, healthcare, industrials, energy, utilities and communication: trade tensions, the pandemic crash, the hiking cycle and the AI wave.
history.scenario.2015.subtitle: Low rates, pandemic, hikes and AI
history.scenario.2015.tip1: Long-term returns come from a few big trends, but the path includes drawdowns beyond 30%.
history.scenario.2015.tip2: Concentrated positions look brilliant in rallies and amplify losses in drawdowns.
history.scenario.2015.tip3: The replay only shows data up to today; do not replace decision-making with hindsight.
history.scenario.2015.title: 2015–2026 Long Cycle
history.scenario.2020.desc: Start at record highs, live through three circuit breakers, zero rates and a historic tech rebound, then the vaccine breakthrough.
history.scenario.2020.subtitle: Circuit breakers, zero rates and a tech bull market
history.scenario.2020.tip1: Crashes move fast; position sizing and a cash buffer matter more than calling the bottom.
history.scenario.2020.tip2: The policy bottom and the market bottom may differ; rebounds often precede economic recovery.
history.scenario.2020.tip3: Different sectors recovered at very different speeds in the same crisis.
history.scenario.2020.title: 2020 Pandemic Crash & Rebound
history.scenario.2022.desc: Replay real US stocks through a hiking cycle: growth valuation compression, bear-market rallies and the year-end low.
history.scenario.2022.subtitle: Inflation, hikes and a growth de-rating
history.scenario.2022.tip1: Rising rates lower the value of distant cash flows; long-duration growth stocks suffer most.
history.scenario.2022.tip2: Bear-market rallies can be violent without a trend reversal.
history.scenario.2022.tip3: Use the replay to test stops and sizing rules, not just hindsight.
history.scenario.2022.title: 2022 Rate-Hike Drawdown

lesson.b1.s1.example.l1: Assets 120m, liabilities 10m and 10m shares give NAV = (120 − 10) / 10 = 11.
lesson.b1.s1.example.l2: If assets rise 10% with unchanged liabilities, NAV becomes 12.1. A 1m-share subscription raises AUM but leaves NAV broadly unchanged.
lesson.b1.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b1.s1.key.text: Return comes from asset performance, not from a larger AUM; growth in size is not investment return.
lesson.b1.s1.key.title: The key distinction
lesson.b1.s1.list.i1: Valuation frequency: mark to market at each close
lesson.b1.s1.list.i2: Dealing price: usually today’s or next-day NAV
lesson.b1.s1.list.i3: Liquidity buffer: hold cash or liquid assets for redemptions
lesson.b1.s1.list.title: Three checks
lesson.b1.s1.p1: NAV = (market value of assets − liabilities) / fund shares. It measures what one fund share is worth, not how large the fund is.
lesson.b1.s1.p2: Subscriptions add shares and assets; redemptions remove both. Market moves change asset value, so NAV changes when the share count is unchanged.
lesson.b1.s1.title: Fund NAV, subscriptions and redemptions
lesson.b1.s2.example.l1: A 60/40 portfolio drifts to 70% stocks; rebalancing sells stocks and buys bonds.
lesson.b1.s2.example.l2: With ±5% bands, weights between 55% and 65% can be left alone, reducing turnover cost.
lesson.b1.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b1.s2.key.text: Rebalancing reduces concentration risk but can give up trend returns and create trading costs; more frequent rebalancing costs more.
lesson.b1.s2.key.title: The trade-off
lesson.b1.s2.list.i1: Volatility target: keep portfolio risk inside the budget
lesson.b1.s2.list.i2: Weight bands: allow small drifts and avoid pointless trades
lesson.b1.s2.list.i3: Cash and liquidity buffer: room for redemptions and opportunities
lesson.b1.s2.list.title: Three tools
lesson.b1.s2.p1: A risk budget allocates total portfolio risk across assets or strategies. It looks at each position’s contribution to volatility, not only at capital weights.
lesson.b1.s2.p2: Rebalancing pulls weights back to their target range, systematically selling what has risen and buying what has fallen to control concentration.
lesson.b1.s2.title: Risk budgeting and rebalancing
lesson.b1.s3.example.l1: The portfolio returns 8% versus a 6% benchmark; 1.2% comes from a tech overweight and 0.8% from selection, with the rest from interaction and fees.
lesson.b1.s3.example.l2: A 0.75% annual fee can cost roughly 7%–8% of terminal value over ten years, depending on the return path.
lesson.b1.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b1.s3.key.text: High return is not proof of good management; evaluate against the mandate, benchmark and risk limits.
lesson.b1.s3.key.title: Judge against the benchmark
lesson.b1.s3.list.i1: Allocation effect: overweighting or underweighting an asset class
lesson.b1.s3.list.i2: Selection effect: stock picking within a class
lesson.b1.s3.list.i3: Fees and cash drag: expenses, taxes and uninvested cash
lesson.b1.s3.list.title: Three sources
lesson.b1.s3.p1: Performance attribution splits return into allocation, selection, interaction and fee drag, answering where the return came from.
lesson.b1.s3.p2: Expense ratios are deducted from NAV over time; client redemptions force asset sales and can amplify trading costs and taxes.
lesson.b1.s3.title: Attribution, fees and redemptions
lesson.b1.s4.example.l1: If the mandate prohibits leverage, a high-conviction stock must be bought with cash rather than margin.
lesson.b1.s4.example.l2: During a concentrated redemption, sell the most liquid assets first instead of dumping core holdings at the worst price.
lesson.b1.s4.example.title: Scenario
lesson.b1.s4.key.text: Stay inside the mandate, then pursue excess return; returns earned by breaking the boundary do not persist.
lesson.b1.s4.key.title: Respect the boundary first
lesson.b1.s4.list.i1: Mandate and IPS: what may and may not be held
lesson.b1.s4.list.i2: Risk limits: volatility, drawdown and concentration caps
lesson.b1.s4.list.i3: Compliance and disclosure: records and conflicts
lesson.b1.s4.list.title: Four constraints
lesson.b1.s4.p1: A mandate defines the investable universe, benchmark, risk limits, liquidity requirements and reporting frequency; the manager is a fiduciary.
lesson.b1.s4.p2: The usual path runs from analyst to portfolio manager to multi-strategy fund or fund founder. More senior roles own risk, attribution and client communication.
lesson.b1.s4.title: Investment mandates and career path
lesson.b2.s1.example.l1: With 12% return, 3% risk-free rate and 18% volatility, Sharpe = (12 − 3) / 18 = 0.5.
lesson.b2.s1.example.l2: The same return with 30% volatility gives Sharpe 0.3, a weaker risk-adjusted result.
lesson.b2.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b2.s1.key.text: Ask whether the sample represents the population before trusting a metric; pretty data may come from a biased sample.
lesson.b2.s1.key.title: Check the sample first
lesson.b2.s1.list.i1: Sample size: short samples give unstable conclusions
lesson.b2.s1.list.i2: Distribution: returns are not normal and tails can be fat
lesson.b2.s1.list.i3: Survivorship bias: only surviving companies remain in the sample
lesson.b2.s1.list.title: Three checks
lesson.b2.s1.p1: Returns are random variables. Describe them with mean, standard deviation, skew and correlation, then infer the population from a sample.
lesson.b2.s1.p2: Sharpe ratio = (annual return − risk-free rate) / annual volatility. It measures excess return per unit of risk but ignores tail risk.
lesson.b2.s1.title: Probability and statistics: from sample to conclusion
lesson.b2.s2.example.l1: Generating today’s signal from the next 20 days of returns makes an absurdly good backtest that cannot be traded.
lesson.b2.s2.example.l2: Adding 0.1% cost and slippage per trade can turn a high-turnover strategy from profit to loss.
lesson.b2.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b2.s2.key.text: A backtest is for falsifying an idea early, not for proving it works; respect out-of-sample failure.
lesson.b2.s2.key.title: The purpose of a backtest
lesson.b2.s2.list.i1: Look-ahead bias: using information not available at the time
lesson.b2.s2.list.i2: Survivorship bias: only still-listed companies remain
lesson.b2.s2.list.i3: Trading costs: commissions, spreads and impact
lesson.b2.s2.list.title: Three biases
lesson.b2.s2.p1: Time series analysis focuses on autocorrelation, volatility clustering and mean reversion; regressing non-stationary data can produce spurious relationships.
lesson.b2.s2.p2: Backtests must avoid look-ahead bias, survivorship bias and ignored trading costs, then validate out-of-sample or with walk-forward tests.
lesson.b2.s2.title: Time series and backtesting
lesson.b2.s3.example.l1: A portfolio has 0.8 value exposure and −0.3 momentum; it gains when value rebounds and loses when momentum persists.
lesson.b2.s3.example.l2: When covariance estimates are unstable, the optimiser can produce extreme weights; constraints and shrinkage help.
lesson.b2.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b2.s3.key.text: An optimiser amplifies your assumptions; bad estimates become extreme positions.
lesson.b2.s3.key.title: The optimiser is an amplifier
lesson.b2.s3.list.i1: Factor exposures: value, momentum, size and others
lesson.b2.s3.list.i2: Covariance matrix: how assets move together
lesson.b2.s3.list.i3: Constraints and turnover: real portfolios cannot adjust freely
lesson.b2.s3.list.title: Three inputs
lesson.b2.s3.p1: Factor models split return into common exposures such as market, industry and style plus idiosyncratic return; alpha is what the factors cannot explain.
lesson.b2.s3.p2: Portfolio optimisation trades expected return against risk and constraints such as no shorting, turnover and sector caps; estimation error gets amplified.
lesson.b2.s3.title: Factor models and portfolio optimisation
lesson.b2.s4.example.l1: A model with 90% training accuracy and 52% out-of-sample accuracy memorised noise rather than a pattern.
lesson.b2.s4.example.l2: Strategy capacity is limited: as capital grows, impact costs can consume the original alpha.
lesson.b2.s4.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b2.s4.key.text: Prove out-of-sample performance before discussing live trading; training performance has no decision value.
lesson.b2.s4.key.title: Out-of-sample first
lesson.b2.s4.list.i2: Regularisation and simpler models: robustness before complexity
lesson.b2.s4.list.i3: Live monitoring and capacity: impact rises with capital
lesson.b2.s4.list.title: Three disciplines
lesson.b2.s4.p1: Machine learning can fit nonlinear relationships, but financial data has a low signal-to-noise ratio and is non-stationary, so overfitting risk is high.
lesson.b2.s4.p2: Cross-validate by time, then monitor drift, trading costs and capacity after deployment.
lesson.b2.s4.title: Machine learning, overfitting and algorithmic trading
lesson.b3.s1.example.l1: For one expiry, a strike-80 put shows 35% IV while a strike-100 put shows 22%, a downward slope.
lesson.b3.s1.example.l2: Short-dated IV rises before earnings; if the move is small, IV falls afterwards and time value decays quickly.
lesson.b3.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b3.s1.key.text: Do not price every strike with one volatility; the surface is the market’s actual quote structure.
lesson.b3.s1.key.title: Do not use one volatility
lesson.b3.s1.list.i1: Skew: low-strike puts are usually more expensive
lesson.b3.s1.list.i2: Term structure: IV changes around events
lesson.b3.s1.list.i3: Surface arbitrage: neighbouring points should not offer riskless profit
lesson.b3.s1.list.title: Three observations
lesson.b3.s1.p1: Black-Scholes assumes one volatility, but the market quotes different implied volatilities for different strikes, creating a smile or skew.
lesson.b3.s1.p2: Plotting IV across strikes and expiries gives the volatility surface; it reflects tail risk, supply and demand, and event expectations.
lesson.b3.s1.title: Volatility smile and surface
lesson.b3.s2.example.l1: Ten calls with 0.5 Delta and a 100 multiplier carry 500 shares of Delta; shorting 500 shares makes the book temporarily neutral.
lesson.b3.s2.example.l2: If Delta rises to 0.6 after a rally, short another 100 shares; frequent rebalancing creates costs.
lesson.b3.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b3.s2.key.text: Delta neutrality is instantaneous; Gamma pulls the book away and requires continuous hedging.
lesson.b3.s2.key.title: Only instantaneously neutral
lesson.b3.s2.list.i2: Gamma risk: Delta changes as price moves
lesson.b3.s2.list.i3: Hedging cost: slippage, commissions and frequent adjustments
lesson.b3.s2.list.title: Three sensitivities
lesson.b3.s2.p1: Delta measures the option price change for a 1-unit move in the underlying; Gamma measures the change in Delta; Vega is volatility sensitivity and Theta is time sensitivity.
lesson.b3.s2.p2: A delta-neutral book buys or sells the underlying to set total Delta to zero; as the underlying moves, the hedge must be rebalanced.
lesson.b3.s2.title: Greeks and dynamic hedging
lesson.b3.s3.example.l1: A bull call spread long 95 and short 105 has maximum loss equal to net premium and capped maximum gain.
lesson.b3.s3.example.l2: A calendar spread long the front month and short the back month benefits when front-month IV falls relative to the back month.
lesson.b3.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b3.s3.key.text: Spreads cap risk but also cap reward; do not treat limited risk as risk-free.
lesson.b3.s3.key.title: Limited risk is not no risk
lesson.b3.s3.list.i1: Vertical spread: same expiry, different strikes
lesson.b3.s3.list.i2: Calendar spread: same strike, different expiries
lesson.b3.s3.list.title: Three structures
lesson.b3.s3.p1: Buying options and dynamically delta hedging can profit when realised volatility exceeds implied volatility; this is gamma scalping.
lesson.b3.s3.p2: Spread strategies combine different strikes or expiries to cap risk and reduce cost; calendar spreads are more sensitive to term structure.
lesson.b3.s3.title: Gamma scalping and spreads
lesson.b3.s4.example.l1: With the underlying down 10% and IV up 15 points, a short-put book can lose far more than a Delta-only estimate suggests.
lesson.b3.s4.example.l2: When volatility spikes, margin requirements rise and forced liquidation can amplify losses.
lesson.b3.s4.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b3.s4.key.text: A stress test is not a forecast; it checks whether the book survives the worst case.
lesson.b3.s4.key.title: Test survival
lesson.b3.s4.list.i1: Joint shocks: price and volatility move together
lesson.b3.s4.list.i2: Liquidity haircut: spreads widen under stress
lesson.b3.s4.list.i3: Model risk: assumptions fail and parameters become unstable
lesson.b3.s4.list.title: Three shocks
lesson.b3.s4.p1: Derivative risk is nonlinear: when price, volatility, time and rates move together, the Greeks themselves change.
lesson.b3.s4.p2: Stress tests should shock price and volatility together and include liquidity haircuts, higher margin and counterparty risk.
lesson.b3.s4.title: Stress testing and career path
lesson.b4.s1.example.l1: Year-1 FCF of 100, 3% growth and 9% WACC give terminal value 100 × 1.03 / (0.09 − 0.03) = 1717.
lesson.b4.s1.example.l2: Raising WACC from 9% to 10% cuts terminal value to 1471; valuation is highly sensitive to the discount rate.

lesson.b4.s1.key.text: DCF output quality depends on assumptions, not the formula; run sensitivity on the key inputs.
lesson.b4.s1.key.title: Assumptions drive the output
lesson.b4.s1.list.i1: Cash flow forecast: revenue, margin and capex
lesson.b4.s1.list.i2: WACC: weighted cost of equity and debt
lesson.b4.s1.list.i3: Terminal value and sensitivity: perpetual growth or exit multiple
lesson.b4.s1.list.title: Three inputs
lesson.b4.s1.p1: DCF discounts future free cash flow to today; the discount rate is usually WACC, reflecting the opportunity cost of equity and debt.
lesson.b4.s1.p2: Terminal value often dominates a DCF; growth, margin and capex assumptions must be internally consistent.
lesson.b4.s1.title: Corporate valuation and DCF
lesson.b4.s2.example.l1: A peer average P/E of 18 and target EPS of 2 imply an indicative value near 36 per share.
lesson.b4.s2.example.l2: Pricing at 30 and closing at 36 on day one is a 20% first-day premium; the underwriter may have underestimated demand.
lesson.b4.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b4.s2.key.text: Multiples give a relative price, not a guarantee of absolute value; peer selection drives the conclusion.
lesson.b4.s2.key.title: Relative, not absolute
lesson.b4.s2.list.i1: Comparable companies: similar business and growth
lesson.b4.s2.list.i2: Precedent transactions: multiples paid in M&A
lesson.b4.s2.list.i3: Bookbuilding and allocation: price from demand
lesson.b4.s2.list.title: Three steps
lesson.b4.s2.p1: Relative valuation uses comparable-company multiples such as P/E, EV/EBITDA or P/S to place the target inside a market pricing framework.
lesson.b4.s2.p2: An IPO runs through preparation, roadshow, bookbuilding and pricing; the underwriter balances demand and valuation, and first-day premiums are common.
lesson.b4.s2.title: Relative valuation and IPOs
lesson.b4.s3.example.l1: Acquirer net income 100, target 30 and synergies 10; an all-stock deal issuing 20 new shares requires comparing merged EPS with standalone EPS.

lesson.b4.s3.key.title: Accretion is not value creation
lesson.b4.s3.list.i1: Leverage and interest coverage: can cash flow service debt?
lesson.b4.s3.list.i2: Synergies: can cost and revenue benefits be delivered?
lesson.b4.s3.list.i3: Exchange ratio and dilution: how many new shares are issued?
lesson.b4.s3.list.title: Three variables
lesson.b4.s3.p1: Debt financing uses leverage to magnify shareholder returns but adds fixed interest and refinancing risk; leverage ratios and covenants are key constraints.
lesson.b4.s3.p2: Whether an acquisition is EPS-accretive depends on synergies, financing and the exchange ratio; issuing new shares dilutes existing owners.
lesson.b4.s3.title: Debt financing, M&A and dilution
lesson.b4.s4.example.l1: A seller wants a higher price while a buyer demands stronger representations and warranties; the deal balances price against risk allocation.
lesson.b4.s4.example.l2: Advising both buyer and seller creates conflicts that must be disclosed or walled off.

lesson.b4.s4.key.text: Deals are not only about price; they also allocate and price risk.
lesson.b4.s4.key.title: Beyond price

lesson.b4.s4.list.i2: Diligence and documents: representations, warranties and indemnities
lesson.b4.s4.list.i3: Negotiation and conflicts: who bears the risk?
lesson.b4.s4.list.title: Three stages
lesson.b4.s4.p1: The IB deal process covers valuation, diligence, structuring, negotiation, board approval and closing; a fairness opinion supports the board’s decision.
lesson.b4.s4.p2: The career path runs analyst → associate → vice president → director/managing director; modelling, industry insight and communication are core skills.
lesson.b4.s4.title: Deal negotiation and career path
lesson.b5.s1.example.l1: A 50bp rate cut saves about 5,000 of annual interest on a 1m floating-rate loan.
lesson.b5.s1.example.l2: If inflation stays high, a cut can push long yields higher, steepen the curve and produce a mixed equity response.
lesson.b5.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b5.s1.key.text: Policy direction is not market direction; prices respond to the surprise versus expectations, not headlines.
lesson.b5.s1.key.title: Surprises drive prices
lesson.b5.s1.list.i1: Policy rate: the central bank’s short-rate anchor
lesson.b5.s1.list.i2: Inflation target: the anchor for policy reaction
lesson.b5.s1.list.i3: Transmission lag: from policy to the real economy and markets
lesson.b5.s1.list.title: Three variables
lesson.b5.s1.p1: Central banks influence funding costs through policy rates, reserve requirements and asset purchases; cuts usually lower discount rates and support risk assets.
lesson.b5.s1.p2: Transmission is lagged: corporate funding, mortgages, FX and asset prices react through different channels, sometimes over months.
lesson.b5.s1.title: Monetary policy and interest rates
lesson.b5.s2.example.l1: Two-year 4.5% and ten-year 3.8% is a 70bp inversion; the market is pricing future cuts or a slowdown.

lesson.b5.s2.key.text: The curve embeds growth and inflation expectations, not just the current rate; inversion is not a precise timing signal.
lesson.b5.s2.key.title: The curve contains expectations
lesson.b5.s2.list.i1: Curve shape: normal, flat or inverted
lesson.b5.s2.list.i2: Breakeven inflation: the market’s inflation expectation
lesson.b5.s2.list.title: Three concepts
lesson.b5.s2.p1: The yield curve connects government bond yields across maturities; a normal curve slopes upward, while inversion is often read as a recession signal.
lesson.b5.s2.p2: Inflation expectations push nominal yields higher; real yield = nominal yield − expected inflation, affecting bond and equity valuation.
lesson.b5.s2.title: Yield curve, inflation and government bonds
lesson.b5.s3.example.l1: Borrowing at 1% to invest at 5% implies 4% annual carry, but a 5% currency depreciation turns it into a loss.
lesson.b5.s3.example.l2: In a global risk-off, a high-yield currency can suffer both narrowing rate differentials and capital outflows.
lesson.b5.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.b5.s3.key.text: Carry earns a premium for bearing tail risk; losses accelerate when the exchange rate reverses.
lesson.b5.s3.key.title: Carry is not free
lesson.b5.s3.list.i1: Rate differential: the gap between two countries’ rates
lesson.b5.s3.list.i2: Carry trade: borrow low-yield, invest high-yield
lesson.b5.s3.list.title: Three drivers
lesson.b5.s3.p1: Exchange rates are driven by rate differentials, inflation, trade balances, capital flows and risk appetite; carry trades borrow in low-yield currencies and invest in high-yield ones.
lesson.b5.s3.p2: When risk appetite falls, capital often returns to the dollar and safe assets, pressuring high-yield currencies and emerging markets.
lesson.b5.s3.title: FX and global capital flows
lesson.b5.s4.example.l1: With slower growth, cooling inflation and a dovish central bank, a portfolio may overweight long-duration bonds and underweight cyclicals.

lesson.b5.s4.list.title: Four dimensions
lesson.b5.s4.p1: Macro traders judge the regime across growth, inflation, policy and liquidity, then express views through bonds, FX, equities or commodities.
lesson.b5.s4.p2: The path runs macro research → strategist → macro fund or multi-asset portfolio manager; data interpretation, models and risk management matter.
lesson.b5.s4.title: Macro trading and career path

lesson.b6.s1.key.title: Liquidity has a price
lesson.b6.s1.list.i1: Best bid and ask: the closest quotes

lesson.b6.s1.title: Order book and bid-ask spread
lesson.b6.s2.example.l1: After buying 10,000 shares, a long-inventory maker may lower the bid and raise the ask to encourage selling.

lesson.b6.s2.key.text: Market-maker profit compensates for risk and liquidity provision; it is not risk-free income.

lesson.u1.s1.example.l2: If you own 1,000 shares, you own 1,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.1% of the company.
lesson.u1.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u1.s1.f1: 1 share = one small slice of company ownership
lesson.u1.s1.f1note: Your percentage of shares determines how much of the company you own.
lesson.u1.s1.key.text: A stock represents a share of ownership in a company. It is not a loan, not a deposit, and it promises no fixed return.
lesson.u1.s1.key.title: Key idea
lesson.u1.s1.myth.text: “Buying stock means lending money to the company, which must pay me back.” That describes a bond. Stocks represent ownership; the company does not promise to repay you.
lesson.u1.s1.myth.title: Common myth
lesson.u1.s1.p1: Imagine you and two friends open a coffee shop with $300,000 of combined capital. You divide ownership into 300,000 equal slices worth $1 each. You put in $90,000, so you own 90,000 slices — 30% of the business. A stock is simply the certificate for those slices.
lesson.u1.s1.p2: To raise money, a company can split ownership into millions or even billions of slices and sell them to the public. Each slice is one share. Buyers become shareholders: they are not lending money to the company, they genuinely own a small piece of it.
lesson.u1.s1.pro.text: An equity security represents a residual claim on a company. After all debts are paid, shareholders share the remaining assets and profits in proportion to their ownership.
lesson.u1.s1.pro.title: Professional definition
lesson.u1.s1.title: A Stock Is a Slice of Ownership
lesson.u1.s2.list.i1: Voting: vote on major company matters in proportion to your shares
lesson.u1.s2.list.i2: Dividends: receive payouts in proportion to your shares
lesson.u1.s2.list.i3: Residual claim: share in what remains after a liquidation pays creditors
lesson.u1.s2.list.i4: Transfer: sell your shares to other investors
lesson.u1.s2.list.title: Four basic shareholder rights
lesson.u1.s2.myth.text: “If the company loses money, shareholders must pay extra.” Normally they do not. Limited liability protects personal assets.
lesson.u1.s2.myth.title: Common myth
lesson.u1.s2.p1: A public company is one whose shares can be bought and sold on a public exchange. Any eligible investor can buy its shares and become one of its owners.
lesson.u1.s2.p2: As a shareholder you have several basic rights: to vote in proportion to your shares at the annual meeting; to receive dividends in proportion to your shares when they are paid; to share in any remaining value after a liquidation pays off debts; and to sell your shares to someone else at any time.
lesson.u1.s2.pro.text: Shareholders can lose at most what they invested. Company debts are not pursued against personal assets (except in cases such as fraud). This limited liability is one reason stock investing became widespread.
lesson.u1.s2.pro.title: Limited liability

lesson.u1.s3.list.title: What exchanges do
lesson.u1.s3.p1: An exchange is an organised marketplace where buyers and sellers post quotes, get matched and trade. The exchange itself does not buy or sell shares; it provides rules, systems and oversight.
lesson.u1.s3.p2: Every listed company has a ticker symbol, such as AURA or VRDN in this game. It works like the stock's ID in the market. Real tickers are usually one to five letters.
lesson.u1.s3.title: Exchanges and Tickers
lesson.u1.s3.warn.text: A company can list on several exchanges with different tickers. A ticker is only an identifier; it says nothing about whether the company is a good investment.

lesson.u1.s4.f1: Market cap = share price × shares outstanding
lesson.u1.s4.f1note: Shares outstanding = every share the company has issued.
lesson.u1.s4.key.text: Share price tells you what one share costs. Market cap tells you what the whole company is worth.
lesson.u1.s4.key.title: The difference
lesson.u1.s4.p1: The share price is the current market price of one share. It updates constantly as buyers and sellers trade: when someone is willing to pay more, the price rises.
lesson.u1.s4.p2: Market capitalisation is the total market value of the whole company: share price × shares outstanding. A high share price does not mean a big company — market cap reflects overall size.

lesson.u1.s4.warn.text: A low share price does not mean a company is cheap. A $5 stock can be more expensive than a $500 stock once you consider market cap, earnings and share count.

lesson.u10.s1.example.l1: The last three closes are $10, $11 and $12.
lesson.u10.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u10.s1.p1: SMA is the arithmetic average of the last N closes. It smooths short-term noise and helps show trend direction.
lesson.u10.s1.p2: Price above a moving average is often described as short-term strength. SMA20 crossing above SMA50 is called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. Both are descriptions, not guarantees.
lesson.u10.s1.title: Moving averages: smoothing noise
lesson.u10.s2.list.i1: Overbought does not mean it must fall now
lesson.u10.s2.list.i2: Strong trends can stay at extremes for a long time
lesson.u10.s2.list.i3: Combine it with trend, volume and fundamentals
lesson.u10.s2.list.title: Using RSI
lesson.u10.s2.p1: RSI compares recent gains and losses on a 0–100 scale. The common thresholds are 70 and 30.
lesson.u10.s2.p2: RSI above 70 means strong recent upward momentum; it may be overbought, or it may stay high in a strong trend. Below 30 is the mirror image.
lesson.u10.s2.title: RSI: momentum and overbought/oversold
lesson.u10.s2.warn.text: Indicators are computed from past prices, lag by construction and cannot predict news or earnings shocks.
lesson.u10.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u10.s3.example.l1: An uptrend with moving averages aligned and RSI in a neutral range is usually more reliable than RSI alone being overbought.
lesson.u10.s3.example.l2: If price breaks below SMA50 on rising volume, the trend may already be weakening.
lesson.u10.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u10.s3.p1: Different parameters produce different signals. SMA20 plus SMA50 is steadier than a single average, but still lags.
lesson.u10.s3.p2: Indicators help confirm trends, size positions and manage risk; they are not a hunt for a guaranteed signal.
lesson.u10.s3.pro.text: Indicators describe, they do not forecast. Any backtest must avoid look-ahead bias and overfitting or the result is meaningless.

lesson.u11.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u11.s1.p1: The income statement starts with revenue, subtracts operating costs and expenses and ends with net income. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue; net margin = net income ÷ revenue.
lesson.u11.s1.p2: EPS = net income ÷ shares outstanding, the denominator of the P/E ratio. The quality of profit growth matters more than a single year.
lesson.u11.s1.title: The income statement: revenue to profit
lesson.u11.s2.f1note: This game's statements are generated from company fundamentals and keep the identity, but are simplified simulations.
lesson.u11.s2.p1: The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a point in time. Assets are what the company owns; liabilities and equity are how it is financed.
lesson.u11.s2.p2: The accounting identity is assets = liabilities + equity. Too much debt raises interest costs and financial risk.
lesson.u11.s2.title: The balance sheet: where assets come from
lesson.u11.s2.warn.text: The statements in this game are simplified teaching simulations, not audited reports, and must not be used for real investment decisions.

lesson.u11.s3.list.i3: Can free cash flow cover dividends and interest?
lesson.u11.s3.list.title: Three checks
lesson.u11.s3.p1: Net income is not cash. Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capital expenditure, and it funds dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
lesson.u11.s3.p2: Check whether profit is backed by cash, whether receivables or inventory are growing unusually, and whether debt is rising quickly.

lesson.u12.s1.example.l1: Simplified: next year's FCF is $100M, the discount rate is 10%, with no terminal value.
lesson.u12.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u12.s1.f1: EV = Σ FCF_t ÷ (1+r)^t + TV ÷ (1+r)^n; TV = FCF_n × (1+g) ÷ (r − g)
lesson.u12.s1.f1note: r is the discount rate, g the perpetual growth rate, and r must exceed g.
lesson.u12.s1.p1: DCF discounts future free cash flow to today's value. The discount rate reflects time value and risk: higher risk means a higher rate and a lower valuation.
lesson.u12.s1.p2: Terminal value usually uses a perpetual growth model. Enterprise value minus net debt gives equity value; divide by shares for value per share.
lesson.u12.s1.title: DCF: discounting future cash back to today
lesson.u12.s2.p1: Growth, discount rate and perpetual growth are extremely sensitive inputs. A small change in assumptions can double or halve value per share.
lesson.u12.s2.p2: Terminal value often dominates enterprise value, so check that perpetual growth stays below long-run economic growth.
lesson.u12.s2.pro.text: DCF is a thinking framework, not a precise answer. Use scenarios (bull, base, bear) instead of a single point estimate.
lesson.u12.s2.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u12.s2.title: Assumptions drive the result
lesson.u12.s3.p1: Valuation gives a range, not an exact price. A margin of safety is the buffer between the purchase price and intrinsic value, absorbing assumption errors.
lesson.u12.s3.p2: DCF can fail for cyclicals, loss-making companies and fast-changing industries. Cross-check with relative valuation and asset value.
lesson.u12.s3.tip.text: Change growth and the discount rate in the demo, watch value per share move, then decide which assumption is least certain.

lesson.u13.s1.example.l2: Real rate = 2.5% − 2% = 0.5%, a relatively loose environment for risk assets.
lesson.u13.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u13.s1.p1: GDP measures an economy's output. Faster growth usually supports corporate earnings, but overheating can bring inflation and rate hikes.
lesson.u13.s1.p2: The cycle moves through expansion, slowdown, recession and recovery. Industrials, materials and discretionary consumer stocks are more cyclical; staples and utilities are more defensive.
lesson.u13.s1.title: Growth, inflation and interest rates
lesson.u13.s2.list.title: What to watch
lesson.u13.s2.p1: Inflation is a broad rise in prices and erodes the purchasing power of cash and fixed income. Moderate inflation often comes with growth; high inflation can force central banks to raise rates.
lesson.u13.s2.p2: Companies with pricing power may pass costs through; cost-sensitive and highly indebted companies feel more pressure.
lesson.u13.s2.title: Inflation and purchasing power
lesson.u13.s2.warn.text: Macro data is revised and lagged; one month does not define a trend. Do not treat a single print as a certain signal.
lesson.u13.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u13.s3.example.l1: With the same cash flows, the discount rate rises from 8% to 10%.
lesson.u13.s3.example.l2: The present value of long-dated cash flow can fall 15–20%, and the valuation contracts.
lesson.u13.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u13.s3.p1: Higher rates raise the cost of capital and the discount rate, usually pressuring equity valuations. High-growth stocks are more sensitive to the discount rate.
lesson.u13.s3.p2: Rate cuts do the opposite; rates also affect bond prices, currencies and corporate funding costs.
lesson.u13.s3.pro.text: Rates connect macro and valuation. Use scenarios (hike / unchanged / cut) rather than betting on one path.
lesson.u13.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u13.s3.title: How rates affect valuation
lesson.u14.s1.example.l2: Weighted expected return is about 5.6% and weighted volatility about 12%; actual portfolio volatility can be lower with diversification.
lesson.u14.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u14.s1.p1: Asset allocation determines the risk and return structure of a portfolio and matters more than any single stock pick. Stocks, bonds and cash have different expected returns and volatility.
lesson.u14.s1.p2: Weights decide the profile: more stocks usually mean higher expected return and volatility; cash lowers volatility but also long-run return.
lesson.u14.s1.title: Asset allocation sets the portfolio's character
lesson.u14.s2.list.title: Checklist
lesson.u14.s2.p1: Lower-correlation assets produce a smoother portfolio; when everything moves together, diversification helps little.
lesson.u14.s2.p2: More holdings is not always better. Over-diversification adds management cost and dilutes conviction; what matters is whether the risks are genuinely different.
lesson.u14.s2.title: Correlation and the limits of diversification
lesson.u14.s2.warn.text: Historical correlations change; in a crisis assets can fall together, and diversification cannot remove systematic risk.
lesson.u14.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u14.s3.example.l1: Target 60% stocks / 40% bonds, but stocks rise to 70%.
lesson.u14.s3.example.l2: Sell about 10% of the portfolio from stocks and buy bonds to return to target.
lesson.u14.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u14.s3.p1: Prices move weights away from target. Rebalancing sells what has grown, buys what has shrunk and restores the intended risk exposure.
lesson.u14.s3.p2: Rebalancing too often raises costs; rebalancing too rarely lets risk drift.
lesson.u14.s3.tip.text: Change stock and bond weights in the allocation demo, then inspect concentration, volatility and max drawdown in Portfolio.
