lesson.u15.s1.example.l1: Account $10,000 with 1% risk = $100; entry $40 and stop $36.
lesson.u15.s1.example.l2: Risk per share is $4, so the position is 100 ÷ 4 = 25 shares, worth $1,000.
lesson.u15.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u15.s1.p1: Define the risk you can accept per trade (for example 1% of the account), then use entry and stop prices to calculate shares.
lesson.u15.s1.p2: Position size = risk amount ÷ risk per share. A wider stop means a smaller position; a tighter stop allows more shares.
lesson.u15.s1.title: Position sizing: risk first, shares second
lesson.u15.s2.list.i1: Set stops and accept gap risk
lesson.u15.s2.list.i3: Hold cash and avoid excessive leverage
lesson.u15.s2.list.title: Basic risk controls
lesson.u15.s2.p1: Drawdown is the fall from a peak in equity. A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to recover.
lesson.u15.s2.p2: A large single position magnifies drawdowns; concentration and correlation determine the portfolio's real risk.
lesson.u15.s2.title: Drawdowns and concentration
lesson.u15.s2.warn.text: Stops can be jumped by gaps and do not guarantee execution at the stop price. A stop is not the absence of risk.
lesson.u15.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u15.s3.example.l1: Two highly correlated trades each risk 1%.
lesson.u15.s3.example.l2: Combined risk is closer to 2% than to a diversified 1%.
lesson.u15.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u15.s3.p1: A risk budget allocates total risk across positions and strategies. When correlation is high, add risk together instead of treating positions as independent.
lesson.u15.s3.p2: The goal of risk management is to survive and preserve the ability to compound, not to win every trade.
lesson.u15.s3.pro.text: Control risk before chasing return. Limiting drawdowns usually matters more than maximising a single trade, because large losses break compounding.
lesson.u15.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u15.s3.title: Risk budgeting and survival
lesson.u16.s1.example.l1: Rising rates often pressure high-valuation growth stocks.
lesson.u16.s1.example.l2: In an economic recovery, cyclical and value styles may outperform.
lesson.u16.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u16.s1.p1: Value buys undervalued assets, growth buys high growth, momentum follows trends and dividend strategies focus on cash returns.
lesson.u16.s1.p2: Every strategy has environments where it works and periods where it fails; none works all the time.
lesson.u16.s1.title: Four common strategies
lesson.u16.s2.list.i1: Define the lookback and rebalance frequency
lesson.u16.s2.list.i3: Avoid look-ahead bias and validate out of sample
lesson.u16.s2.list.title: Momentum design
lesson.u16.s2.p1: Momentum buys recent winners and sells recent losers, assuming trends persist.
lesson.u16.s2.p2: In choppy markets momentum gets whipsawed; it needs cost, turnover and stop-loss discipline.
lesson.u16.s2.title: Momentum and trend
lesson.u16.s2.warn.text: Past momentum is not future momentum; a strong backtest can be overfitting or an in-sample illusion.
lesson.u16.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u16.s3.example.l1: Value plus dividend strategies are usually more defensive.
lesson.u16.s3.example.l2: Growth plus momentum is more aggressive in bull markets, with potentially larger drawdowns.
lesson.u16.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u16.s3.p1: Strategies can be combined, but watch overlapping holdings and rising correlation.
lesson.u16.s3.p2: Define entry, exit, sizing and risk with rules instead of trading on feelings.

lesson.u17.s1.example.l2: Cover at $40 for $4,000, locking in $1,000 before costs.
lesson.u17.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u17.s1.p1: Short selling borrows shares and sells them, hoping to buy them back lower. You profit from the gap between the sale price and the repurchase price, not from company growth.
lesson.u17.s1.p2: The flow: borrow from the broker, sell at market, buy back (cover) after a decline, then return the shares and pay borrowing costs. Until you cover, you owe those shares.
lesson.u17.s1.title: How short selling works
lesson.u17.s1.warn.text: Short losses have no theoretical ceiling because the price can rise far above your sale price. Insufficient margin triggers forced liquidation.
lesson.u17.s1.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u17.s2.info.text: The simulation requires 50% of the short market value as collateral. Dividends are deducted as a liability; the borrow fee is not charged separately yet.
lesson.u17.s2.info.title: Simplified in this game
lesson.u17.s2.list.title: Main costs of a short
lesson.u17.s2.p1: Short proceeds are usually not free to spend; they serve as collateral. The broker also requires extra margin to cover the risk of a rising price.
lesson.u17.s2.p2: Borrowing shares has a fee, and if the company pays a dividend the short seller owes it. A rising price erodes collateral and can trigger a margin call.
lesson.u17.s2.title: Costs and collateral
lesson.u17.s3.example.l1: Short $2,000 of stock; a 50% rally loses $1,000.
lesson.u17.s3.example.l2: If that position used only 50% collateral, account equity is hit hard.
lesson.u17.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u17.s3.p1: You can cover voluntarily, or the broker can force a buy-in when margin runs short. Planning the stop and position size matters more than calling the exact top.
lesson.u17.s3.p2: Shorting expresses an overvaluation view or hedges a long, but it is a poor long-term hold: borrow costs, dividends and squeeze risk keep accumulating.
lesson.u17.s3.pro.text: Shorts usually pair with strict stops and event-driven research. In illiquid names, a short squeeze can make covering dramatically more expensive.
lesson.u17.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u17.s3.title: When to cover
lesson.u18.s1.example.l1: With $10,000 of your own cash, buy $15,000 of stock using a $5,000 loan: 1.5x leverage.
lesson.u18.s1.example.l2: A 10% price drop loses about $1,500 of equity, which is 15% of your own cash.
lesson.u18.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u18.s1.p1: A margin account lets you borrow cash to buy more stock, and uses short proceeds as collateral. Leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
lesson.u18.s1.p2: Initial margin sets how large a position you may open; maintenance margin is the minimum equity the account must retain.
lesson.u18.s1.title: Margin accounts and leverage
lesson.u18.s2.formula: Daily interest = debit balance × annual rate ÷ 252
lesson.u18.s2.list.title: What drives financing cost
lesson.u18.s2.note: This simulation uses an 8% annual rate and 252 trading days as a teaching assumption.
lesson.u18.s2.p1: The debit balance accrues interest daily, usually by converting an annual rate to each trading day. The longer you hold, the more interest accumulates.
lesson.u18.s2.p2: Interest directly reduces cash and equity. Even with a flat price, a leveraged position slowly bleeds.
lesson.u18.s2.title: Financing interest
lesson.u18.s3.example.l1: After a margin purchase, the stock falls 35%.
lesson.u18.s3.example.l2: Equity may fall below the maintenance requirement and all positions are liquidated.
lesson.u18.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u18.s3.p1: When equity falls below the maintenance requirement the account gets a margin call. If it cannot be met, the broker forces positions to be sold.
lesson.u18.s3.p2: Forced liquidation usually happens at an unfavourable price, turning paper losses into permanent ones. Higher leverage makes the trigger easier to hit.
lesson.u18.s3.title: Maintenance and forced liquidation
lesson.u18.s3.warn.text: Leverage does not raise your win rate; it only amplifies outcomes. Start small to learn how interest and liquidation work.
lesson.u18.s3.warn.title: Leverage cuts both ways
lesson.u19.s1.example.l1: Buy at $100 and place a sell stop at $92.
lesson.u19.s1.example.l2: When the price falls through $92 the order triggers and fills at the prevailing bid.
lesson.u19.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u19.s1.p1: A stop order becomes a market order once the trigger price is reached. Sell stops protect longs; buy stops protect shorts.
lesson.u19.s1.p2: Place the trigger where you genuinely accept that the thesis is wrong, not at an arbitrary level. The fill can differ from the trigger.
lesson.u19.s1.title: Stop orders
lesson.u19.s2.example.l1: Buy at $100 with a $6 trail; at $120 the stop moves up to $114.
lesson.u19.s2.example.l2: A pullback triggers the exit but still locks in $14 before costs.
lesson.u19.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u19.s2.list.title: Before setting a trailing stop
lesson.u19.s2.p1: A trailing stop tightens as the price moves favourably but never loosens. It combines letting profits run with locking in part of the gain.
lesson.u19.s2.p2: The trail can be set as a dollar amount. Volatile stocks need a wider distance, otherwise normal noise knocks you out.
lesson.u19.s2.title: Trailing stops
lesson.u19.s3.example.l1: The stop is at $50, but the next open gaps to $42.
lesson.u19.s3.example.l2: The market stop fills near $42, far below the trigger.
lesson.u19.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u19.s3.p1: A stop order does not guarantee the stop price. On a gap down or with thin liquidity, the fill can be materially worse.
lesson.u19.s3.p2: A stop-limit can cap the price but may not fill at all; a market stop guarantees an exit but not a price.
lesson.u19.s3.pro.text: Use position size to absorb gap risk and stops to limit everyday drawdown; they cannot replace each other.
lesson.u19.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u19.s3.title: Execution, gaps and slippage
lesson.u19.s3.warn.text: In extreme conditions stops trigger together and slippage widens. Never treat a stop as risk-free insurance.
lesson.u19.s3.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u2.s1.example.l1: You buy 20 shares at $50 with $1,000 and pay a $1 commission.
lesson.u2.s1.example.l2: Your position grows by 20 shares and your cash falls by $1,001. The money did not vanish; it changed from cash into stock.
lesson.u2.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u2.s1.list.i2: Choose the order type (market or limit)
lesson.u2.s1.list.i5: Your cash and positions update after the fill
lesson.u2.s1.list.title: Five steps of a trade
lesson.u2.s1.myth.text: “The money disappears after I buy.” It becomes stock. Apart from the fee, total assets simply change form.
lesson.u2.s1.myth.title: Common myth
lesson.u2.s1.p1: You place an order through a broker. The broker sends it to an exchange, where the trading system matches it. When a buyer and seller agree on a price, the trade executes.
lesson.u2.s1.p2: Buying means you gain shares and pay cash. Selling means you give up shares and receive cash. When the price rises, the same shares sell for more; when it falls, for less.
lesson.u2.s1.title: How a Buy or Sell Happens
lesson.u2.s2.example.l1: Start with $10,000 cash, then buy $5,000 of stock and pay a $1 commission.
lesson.u2.s2.example.l2: Cash becomes $4,999, the position is worth $5,000, and total equity is about $9,999.
lesson.u2.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u2.s2.f1: Total equity = cash + Σ (shares × current price)
lesson.u2.s2.key.text: Total equity = cash + the market value of all positions. Price changes move total equity, not cash.
lesson.u2.s2.key.title: Remember this identity
lesson.u2.s2.p1: A trading account holds two things: cash and positions. Cash is buying power you can use immediately. A position is the quantity of shares you own and what they cost.
lesson.u2.s2.p2: When you buy, cash falls and the position grows. When you sell, the position shrinks and cash rises. Ignoring fees, total equity is unchanged at the moment of the trade.
lesson.u2.s2.title: Cash, Positions and Total Equity
lesson.u2.s2.warn.text: Fees reduce total equity slightly. That is a real cost of trading, not a system error.
lesson.u2.s2.warn.title: Keep in mind
lesson.u2.s3.example.l1: The last price is $50.00, with a bid of $49.98 and an ask of $50.02.
lesson.u2.s3.example.l2: A market buy of 10 shares fills at $50.02, not $50.00. The difference is the spread cost.
lesson.u2.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u2.s3.list.i3: Slippage is possible when liquidity is thin or volatility is high
lesson.u2.s3.list.title: Three traits of market orders
lesson.u2.s3.p1: A market order asks to trade immediately at the best price currently available. It prioritises speed of execution, not a specific price.
lesson.u2.s3.p2: The “last price” you see is the price of the previous trade, not necessarily your next fill. Buys usually execute at the ask; sells usually execute at the bid.
lesson.u2.s3.title: Market Orders and Execution Price
lesson.u2.s3.warn.text: With volatile or thinly traded stocks, a market order can fill far from the price you saw. That is slippage.
lesson.u2.s3.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u2.s4.example.l1: Bid $49.98, ask $50.02, so the spread is $0.04.
lesson.u2.s4.example.l2: Buy 100 shares and sell immediately and the spread alone costs about $4 (before commission).
lesson.u2.s4.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u2.s4.f1: Spread = ask − bid; spread cost ≈ spread × quantity
lesson.u2.s4.p1: The bid is the highest price a buyer will currently pay. The ask is the lowest price a seller will currently accept. The gap between them is the spread.
lesson.u2.s4.p2: The spread is an implicit trading cost: buy and immediately sell, and you usually lose a little to the spread. More liquid, actively traded stocks usually have tighter spreads.
lesson.u2.s4.tip.text: Check the bid and ask in the quote strip on the Trading page, and compare them before and after you place an order.
lesson.u2.s4.tip.title: Try it
lesson.u2.s4.title: Bid, Ask and the Spread
lesson.u20.s1.example.l1: Bid $49.99 and ask $50.01: the spread is $0.02.
lesson.u20.s1.example.l2: Buying 100 shares immediately costs about $2 in spread.
lesson.u20.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u20.s1.p1: The order book lists bids and asks by price. The gap between the best bid and the best ask is the spread.
lesson.u20.s1.p2: The spread is the immediate cost of trading. Better liquidity usually means a tighter spread; small or obscure names trade wider.
lesson.u20.s1.title: The order book and the spread
lesson.u20.s2.list.title: Signals to watch
lesson.u20.s2.p1: Depth is the quantity available at each price. A large order eats several levels, so the average fill moves away from the best quote: that is slippage.
lesson.u20.s2.p2: Liquidity also depends on time, news and volatility. Around the open, the close and major events, depth can thin out quickly.
lesson.u20.s2.title: Depth, liquidity and slippage
lesson.u20.s2.warn.text: This simulated book is derived from the quote for teaching. Real depth changes quickly and includes hidden orders.
lesson.u20.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u20.s3.example.l1: Buy 2,500 shares when the first two levels hold only 1,500.
lesson.u20.s3.example.l2: The remaining 1,000 keep lifting offers, so the average price sits above the best ask.
lesson.u20.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u20.s3.p1: Orders larger than visible depth push the price up (or down). Slicing orders, using limits and spreading execution over time reduce impact.
lesson.u20.s3.p2: Limit orders protect price but may only fill partially; market orders prioritise completion and pay with slippage.
lesson.u20.s3.pro.text: Evaluate both price and probability of completion. Large capital cares more about market impact than a single commission.
lesson.u20.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u20.s3.title: Large orders and market impact
lesson.u21.s1.example.l1: AURA trades at $50; a 30-day $55 call costs $1.20.
lesson.u21.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u21.s1.list.title: Every option contract specifies
lesson.u21.s1.p1: An option gives the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at the strike on expiry. The buyer pays a premium for that right.
lesson.u21.s1.p2: A contract usually covers 100 shares; the expiry sets how long the right lasts. This game uses European options that can only be exercised at expiry.
lesson.u21.s1.title: The four contract terms
lesson.u21.s2.info.text: Only buying is supported for now: hold to expiry or close early at the model value. Selling options and multi-leg strategies come later.
lesson.u21.s2.info.title: Scope of this game
lesson.u21.s2.p1: A call gives the buyer the right to buy the underlying at the strike; a put gives the right to sell it at the strike.
lesson.u21.s2.p2: Buyers pay the premium and have limited loss; sellers collect the premium but carry the obligation. This stage is long-only.
lesson.u21.s2.title: Calls and puts
lesson.u21.s3.example.l1: Spot $52 and a $50 call have $2 of intrinsic value.
lesson.u21.s3.example.l2: If the premium is $3.10, time value is $3.10 − $2 = $1.10.
lesson.u21.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u21.s3.p1: The strike determines intrinsic value: a call is worth max(spot − strike, 0); a put is the reverse.
lesson.u21.s3.p2: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value shrinks toward expiry and grows with volatility.
lesson.u21.s3.title: Strike and premium
lesson.u21.s3.warn.text: The premium can go to zero. The buyer’s maximum loss is the premium paid, but that does not raise the odds of winning.
lesson.u21.s3.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u22.s1.example.l1: A $50 strike call costs $2, so one contract costs $200.
lesson.u22.s1.example.l2: At expiry the stock is $60: intrinsic $10 × 100 = $1,000, a $800 profit.
lesson.u22.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u22.s1.p1: A long call expresses a bullish view. A small premium controls 100 shares, so both gains and losses are amplified.
lesson.u22.s1.p2: A rally magnifies the payoff; without a rally the premium can expire worthless. Time hurts buyers, volatility helps them.
lesson.u22.s1.title: The logic of buying calls
lesson.u22.s2.example.l1: A $50 strike call with a $2 premium breaks even at $52.
lesson.u22.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u22.s2.formula: Expiry P&L = max(S − K, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium
lesson.u22.s2.list.i1: How far the strike sits from spot
lesson.u22.s2.list.i2: Premium as a share of the account
lesson.u22.s2.list.i3: Whether a catalyst remains before expiry
lesson.u22.s2.list.title: Check before buying a call
lesson.u22.s2.note: S is the expiry price and K the strike; commissions and taxes are excluded.
lesson.u22.s2.p1: Expiry P&L = max(spot − strike, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium paid.
lesson.u22.s2.p2: Breakeven = strike + premium per share. The stock must finish above that level for the buyer to profit.
lesson.u22.s2.title: Payoff and breakeven
lesson.u22.s3.p1: Theta erodes the premium every day and accelerates near expiry. Even a correct direction can lose money if it takes too long.
lesson.u22.s3.p2: A drop in implied volatility also lowers the premium, which can offset a rally in the underlying.
lesson.u22.s3.pro.text: Size positions to cap premium spend and treat options as limited-risk expressions, not a sure path to leverage.
lesson.u22.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u22.s3.title: Time and volatility
lesson.u22.s3.warn.text: Buying a call is not a guaranteed bullish trade. The stock must rise enough, fast enough, to beat time decay.
lesson.u22.s3.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u23.s1.example.l1: A $50 strike put costs $2, so one contract costs $200.
lesson.u23.s1.example.l2: At expiry the stock is $40: intrinsic $10 × 100 = $1,000, an $800 profit.
lesson.u23.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u23.s1.p1: A long put gives the right to sell at the strike, so its value rises when the underlying falls.
lesson.u23.s1.p2: Puts can speculate on a decline or insure an existing holding; the premium is the insurance cost.
lesson.u23.s1.title: The logic of buying puts
lesson.u23.s2.example.l1: A $50 strike put with a $2 premium breaks even at $48.
lesson.u23.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u23.s2.formula: Expiry P&L = max(K − S, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium
lesson.u23.s2.list.i1: How far the stock must fall to profit
lesson.u23.s2.list.i2: Whether the premium is fair insurance
lesson.u23.s2.list.i3: Whether the expiry gives enough time
lesson.u23.s2.list.title: Check before buying a put
lesson.u23.s2.note: S is the expiry price and K the strike; commissions and taxes are excluded.
lesson.u23.s2.p1: Expiry P&L = max(strike − spot, 0) × 100 × contracts − premium paid.
lesson.u23.s2.p2: Breakeven = strike − premium per share. The stock must finish below that level for the buyer to profit.
lesson.u23.s2.title: Put payoff
lesson.u23.s3.example.l1: Hold $10,000 of stock and buy a $45 strike put for $200.
lesson.u23.s3.example.l2: If the stock crashes, the maximum loss is capped by the strike and the premium.
lesson.u23.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u23.s3.p1: Stock plus a long put is a protective put: downside is capped, at the cost of the premium.
lesson.u23.s3.p2: Insurance is not free. Continuous protection drags on long-term returns, but it helps around uncertain events.
lesson.u23.s3.pro.text: Compare insurance cost with the drawdown you can tolerate. Do not over-insure noise, but do not stay naked into major events either.
lesson.u23.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u23.s3.title: Protective puts
lesson.u24.s1.example.l1: Spot $52 and a $50 call have $2 of intrinsic value.
lesson.u24.s1.example.l2: At a $3.10 premium, time value is $1.10 and shrinks toward expiry.
lesson.u24.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u24.s1.p1: Premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value reflects the possibility of future moves.
lesson.u24.s1.p2: Implied volatility is the market’s price for future movement. Higher volatility makes options more expensive.
lesson.u24.s1.title: Intrinsic and time value
lesson.u24.s2.formula: Call = S · N(d1) − K · e^(−rT) · N(d2)
lesson.u24.s2.list.title: Five inputs
lesson.u24.s2.note: This game uses a 4% risk-free rate and simulated company volatility; results are teaching estimates only.
lesson.u24.s2.p1: The model prices European options from spot, strike, time to expiry, volatility and the risk-free rate.
lesson.u24.s2.p2: Volatility and time matter most to buyers; rates have a smaller effect.
lesson.u24.s2.title: The five Black-Scholes inputs
lesson.u24.s3.list.i2: Gamma: speed of change in delta
lesson.u24.s3.list.i4: Vega: effect of a 1 point volatility move
lesson.u24.s3.list.i5: Rho: effect of a 1 point rate move
lesson.u24.s3.list.title: The five Greeks
lesson.u24.s3.p1: Delta measures how much the premium moves for a $1 move in the underlying; gamma measures how fast delta changes.
lesson.u24.s3.p2: Theta is time decay, vega is volatility sensitivity and rho is rate sensitivity.
lesson.u24.s3.pro.text: Use Greeks to manage portfolio risk, not to predict direction. Watch delta and theta first, then volatility exposure.
lesson.u24.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u24.s3.title: The Greeks
lesson.u25.s1.example.l1: Sell one $50 call for $2 and collect $200.
lesson.u25.s1.example.l2: At expiry the stock is $60: pay $10 × 100 = $1,000, a net loss of $800.
lesson.u25.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u25.s1.p1: Selling an option collects premium immediately but transfers the obligation to the buyer. The buyer chooses whether to exercise.
lesson.u25.s1.p2: A short call’s maximum profit is the premium while its loss can be far larger; a short put’s maximum loss is the strike minus premium.
lesson.u25.s1.title: Selling options for premium
lesson.u25.s2.list.i1: Whether cash or shares cover the obligation
lesson.u25.s2.list.i3: Whether you accept buying or delivering at the strike
lesson.u25.s2.list.title: Check before selling
lesson.u25.s2.p1: Short options need collateral: a cash-secured put reserves strike × 100 in cash, while uncovered calls need extra margin.
lesson.u25.s2.p2: In-the-money short options are assigned at expiry. This game cash-settles intrinsic value; real brokers may deliver stock.
lesson.u25.s2.title: Collateral and assignment
lesson.u25.s2.warn.text: A naked call has no theoretical loss limit. Do not confuse a high win rate with low risk.
lesson.u25.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u25.s3.example.l1: Sell a $2 put; if the stock finishes flat the premium expires worthless.
lesson.u25.s3.example.l2: The gain is $200 before collateral costs, but a break below the strike changes the picture fast.
lesson.u25.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u25.s3.p1: Time favours sellers: theta erodes option value every day, so the contract can be bought back cheaper.
lesson.u25.s3.p2: Rising volatility, gaps and event risk can still expand losses quickly, so position size is critical.
lesson.u25.s3.pro.text: Selling is risk management, not prediction. Define the maximum loss first, then judge the return.
lesson.u25.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u25.s3.title: The seller’s time advantage
lesson.u26.s1.example.l1: Hold 100 shares at $50 and sell a $55 call for $1.50.
lesson.u26.s1.example.l2: Below $55 you keep the shares and $150; above $55 the shares are delivered at $55.
lesson.u26.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u26.s1.p1: Hold 100 shares and sell one call to create a covered call: the stock covers delivery in exchange for premium.
lesson.u26.s1.p2: A strong rally caps upside because the shares are called away; a decline is only partly cushioned by premium.
lesson.u26.s1.title: Covered calls: rent out your shares
lesson.u26.s2.example.l1: Sell a $45 put for $1.20 and reserve $4,500 cash.
lesson.u26.s2.example.l2: Above $45 you keep $120; below $45 you buy at $45, an effective cost of $43.80.

lesson.u26.s2.list.i1: You are happy to own the stock
lesson.u26.s2.list.i2: The strike is below your fair value estimate
lesson.u26.s2.list.title: When it fits
lesson.u26.s2.p1: Sell a put and reserve strike × 100 in cash: you collect premium in exchange for a possible purchase at the strike.
lesson.u26.s2.p2: Below the strike you buy at the strike; above the strike the premium is yours.
lesson.u26.s2.title: Cash-secured puts: willing to buy
lesson.u26.s3.p1: Covered calls and CSPs raise the win rate and lower volatility, but give up upside or cash flexibility.
lesson.u26.s3.p2: They work well in range-bound markets and can lag simple ownership in strong trends.
lesson.u26.s3.pro.text: Treat income strategies as position management tools, not a promise of steady cash flow.
lesson.u26.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u26.s3.title: The trade-off in income strategies
lesson.u26.s3.warn.text: Premium is not free income. Assignment, missed upside and opportunity cost are real costs.

lesson.u27.s1.example.l1: Buy the $50 call for $3 and sell the $55 call for $1: net debit $2.
lesson.u27.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u27.s1.p1: Buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call: that is a bull call spread.
lesson.u27.s1.p2: The short leg lowers the debit and caps upside. Maximum loss is the net debit; maximum profit is the strike width minus that debit.
lesson.u27.s1.title: Bull call spreads
lesson.u27.s2.formula: Maximum profit = (strike width − net debit) × 100 × contracts
lesson.u27.s2.list.i2: Make sure the net debit is affordable
lesson.u27.s2.list.i3: Check whether the capped profit justifies the risk
lesson.u27.s2.list.title: When building a spread
lesson.u27.s2.note: Both legs share an expiry and opposite sides; a positive net debit means you pay up front.
lesson.u27.s2.p1: Buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put: that is a bear put spread.
lesson.u27.s2.p2: The short leg lowers cost and keeps risk defined while expressing a bearish view.
lesson.u27.s2.title: Bear put spreads
lesson.u27.s3.info.text: Strategy cards pick two legs with the same expiry and different strikes, then validate cash against the net debit.
lesson.u27.s3.info.title: In this game
lesson.u27.s3.p1: Spreads cut premium cost and define maximum loss, which suits traders with a directional view who do not want to pay for a single leg.
lesson.u27.s3.p2: The trade-off is capped profit; a huge move can leave the spread far behind a naked option.
lesson.u27.s3.pro.text: A spread is a risk-budget tool. Size from maximum loss first, then decide whether the capped return is enough.
lesson.u27.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u27.s3.title: Why use spreads
lesson.u28.s1.example.l1: A $50 straddle with a $2 call and a $2 put costs $400.
lesson.u28.s1.example.l2: Breakevens are $54 and $46, so the stock must move a long way.
lesson.u28.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u28.s1.p1: Buy a call and a put with the same strike and expiry: that is a long straddle, a bet on large movement rather than direction.
lesson.u28.s1.p2: Maximum loss is the two premiums; either direction can profit, but the move must clear the breakevens.
lesson.u28.s1.title: Long straddles
lesson.u28.s2.example.l1: A $55 call for $1 and a $45 put for $1 cost $200.
lesson.u28.s2.example.l2: The stock must exceed $56 or fall below $44 to profit.

lesson.u28.s2.list.title: Before buying volatility
lesson.u28.s2.p1: Buy an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put: that is a long strangle, cheaper but needing a larger move.
lesson.u28.s2.p2: The breakeven range is wider, which suits big events where at-the-money premium is too expensive.
lesson.u28.s2.title: Long strangles
lesson.u28.s3.p1: Long volatility fights time decay and falling implied volatility; a flat market erodes both legs.
lesson.u28.s3.p2: Buying when implied volatility is high means even a move can be offset by an IV collapse.
lesson.u28.s3.pro.text: Compare implied with historical volatility before an event. Expensive volatility needs an extreme move to pay.
lesson.u28.s3.pro.title: Professional view
lesson.u28.s3.title: The risk in volatility trades
lesson.u28.s3.warn.text: A straddle is not “profit either way”. The buyer only wins if movement exceeds what the market already priced.

lesson.u29.s1.list.title: Contract terms
lesson.u29.s1.p1: A future is an agreement to buy or sell the underlying at a set price on a future date. Longs face rising prices; shorts face falling prices.
lesson.u29.s1.p2: Each contract covers 100 shares. Opening requires roughly 15% margin, but P&L is calculated on the full notional.
lesson.u29.s1.title: Futures contracts and margin
lesson.u29.s2.formula: Daily variation = (settlement − prior settlement) × direction × contracts × 100
lesson.u29.s2.note: Direction is +1 for longs and −1 for shorts; this game applies it at each day close.
lesson.u29.s2.p1: Futures settle to the latest price every day: gains are credited to cash and losses are debited as variation margin.
lesson.u29.s2.p2: Leverage means small price moves can change equity dramatically, and repeated losses can exhaust margin.
lesson.u29.s2.title: Daily mark-to-market
lesson.u29.s2.warn.text: Futures are not free leverage. Losses can exceed the initial margin.
lesson.u29.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u29.s3.example.l1: Spot $50 and a 60-day future at $50.33 give a $0.33 basis.
lesson.u29.s3.example.l2: At expiry the basis converges to zero and futures equal spot.
lesson.u29.s3.example.title: Worked example

lesson.u3.s1.p1: Cost basis is the total amount you paid for a position, including the purchase price and the buy commission. Average cost = cost basis ÷ shares held.
lesson.u3.s1.p2: Market value = current price × shares held. The difference between the two is your unrealized profit or loss.

lesson.u3.s2.key.title: One-line summary
lesson.u3.s2.p1: Unrealized P&L is the gain or loss while you still hold the shares; it moves with the price. Realized P&L is locked in once you sell.
lesson.u3.s2.p2: While you hold, the P&L is only a book number. Selling converts it into cash. Realized gains add cash; realized losses reduce it.

lesson.u3.s3.p1: Return expresses P&L as a percentage of the capital invested: return = P&L ÷ cost × 100%.
lesson.u3.s3.p2: Returns let you compare trades of different sizes: $100 profit is 10% on $1,000 of capital, but only 0.1% on $100,000.

lesson.u3.s4.p1: A commission is a service fee charged by a broker or platform. It can be a flat amount per order or a percentage of the traded value.
lesson.u3.s4.p2: Fees come out of your cash and directly reduce gains or deepen losses. Trading frequently turns fees into a significant drag — one reason overtrading is a problem.

lesson.u4.s1.p1: Real markets have fixed sessions (for example, US equities trade 09:30–16:00 Eastern Time) and are closed on weekends and holidays. Nothing executes while the market is closed.
lesson.u4.s1.p2: This game uses a simulated clock: each trading day has eight time steps. You can pause, run at 1× / 5× / 20×, or fast-forward to the next session. Orders only match while the market is running.

lesson.u4.s2.list.title: Market orders
lesson.u4.s2.p1: A market order is the simplest instruction: fill immediately at the best available price. It suits situations where execution matters more than price.
lesson.u4.s2.p2: The trade-off is price uncertainty. You control quantity and direction, not the fill price.
lesson.u4.s2.title: Market Orders: Pros and Costs
lesson.u4.s3.example.l1: With the market at $50, you place a buy limit for 100 shares at $48.
lesson.u4.s3.example.l2: It only fills if the ask drops to $48 or lower. If the stock keeps rising, the order may never fill.
lesson.u4.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u4.s3.f1: Buy limit: fill ≤ limit; sell limit: fill ≥ limit
lesson.u4.s3.list.i1: Limit below the market: rests in the order book waiting for a pullback
lesson.u4.s3.list.i2: Limit above the market: may fill immediately at a better prevailing price
lesson.u4.s3.list.title: Two behaviours for buy limits
lesson.u4.s3.p1: A limit order sets the maximum price you will pay (buy) or the minimum you will accept (sell). It only fills at that price or better.
lesson.u4.s3.p2: Buy limits sit below the market, waiting for a pullback; sell limits sit above the market, waiting for a rally. Limit orders guarantee price, not execution.
lesson.u4.s3.title: Limit Orders
lesson.u4.s3.warn.text: Limit orders can miss opportunities: if the price never returns to your level, you stay in cash while the stock rallies.
lesson.u4.s3.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u4.s4.p1: Orders have states: open, filled, cancelled and rejected. An unfilled limit order rests in the order book until it fills or you cancel it.
lesson.u4.s4.p2: Liquidity describes how easily a stock trades and how close fills are to the expected price. Active stocks have good liquidity, tight spreads and less price impact from size.
lesson.u4.s4.p3: Large orders can sweep several price levels and cause market impact, worsening the average fill. This game simplifies execution to the top of book, but spreads and slippage still exist.

lesson.u5.s1.example.l1: You hold 100 shares and the dividend is $0.60 per share, so you receive $60 in cash.
lesson.u5.s1.example.l2: The price was $40.00 before the ex-date and adjusts to about $39.40, reducing the position value by about $60.
lesson.u5.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u5.s1.f1: Cash dividend = shares held × dividend per share
lesson.u5.s1.f1note: This game pays quarterly: dividend per share = starting price × annual yield ÷ 4.
lesson.u5.s1.key.text: Dividends come from company profits and cash flow. They are not guaranteed: a company can cut, suspend or cancel them.
lesson.u5.s1.key.title: Key idea
lesson.u5.s1.myth.text: "A higher yield is always better" is false. A high yield can come from a falling share price or from a one-off payout that cannot last.
lesson.u5.s1.myth.title: Common myth
lesson.u5.s1.p1: When a company earns money it can reinvest it in the business or pay part of the cash out to shareholders. The latter is a dividend, also called a cash distribution.
lesson.u5.s1.p2: A dividend is not free money: on the ex-dividend date the share price usually adjusts down by roughly the dividend per share. You receive cash while the market value of your holding falls, so total value is broadly unchanged at that instant.
lesson.u5.s1.title: Cash dividends: sharing profits with shareholders
lesson.u5.s2.example.l1: Annual dividend per share is $1.20 and the price is $40.00, so the yield is 1.20 ÷ 40 = 3.00%.
lesson.u5.s2.example.l2: If the price falls to $30.00 the yield becomes 4.00%, but the company still pays $1.20 per share.
lesson.u5.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u5.s2.f1: Dividend yield = annual dividend per share ÷ current price × 100%
lesson.u5.s2.f1note: Yield moves with the share price; the dividend per share is usually declared quarterly.

lesson.u5.s2.list.i2: The share price rises or falls

lesson.u5.s2.list.title: Why the yield changes
lesson.u5.s2.p1: Dividend yield links the dividend per share to the share price. It tells you what percentage of cash income you would receive in a year at the current price.
lesson.u5.s2.p2: When the price falls, the same dividend per share produces a higher yield. That does not mean the company became more generous; the shares became cheaper, which may also signal rising risk.
lesson.u5.s2.title: Dividend yield: putting the payout next to the price
lesson.u5.s2.warn.text: Dividend yield is not a fixed interest rate. The company may cut the payout and the price may keep falling; both affect your real return.
lesson.u5.s2.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u5.s3.example.l1: You hold 200 shares and the dividend is $0.50 per share, so you receive $100 on the ex-date.
lesson.u5.s3.example.l2: The price moves from $25.00 to about $24.50, leaving total value broadly unchanged at that instant.
lesson.u5.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u5.s3.p1: After declaring a dividend the company sets a record date and an ex-dividend date. In the standard convention, holders before the ex-date receive the payment; buyers on or after the ex-date do not.
lesson.u5.s3.p2: This game simplifies the process: at the close of the ex-date it credits cash to your account and adjusts the share price down by roughly the dividend amount. You see cash rise and position value fall.
lesson.u5.s3.tip.text: Use the demo below to change shares, price and yield, then watch annual cash flow and the ten-year reinvestment result.

lesson.u5.s3.title: The ex-dividend date: cash in exchange for price
lesson.u5.s3.warn.text: Taxes, trading costs and price moves around the ex-date mean receiving a dividend is not the same as gaining that amount. This game does not model dividend taxes.

lesson.u5.s4.example.l1: EPS is $2.00 and the annual dividend is $1.00, so the payout ratio is 50%.
lesson.u5.s4.example.l2: Half of earnings goes to shareholders; the other half stays in the business for growth or debt reduction.
lesson.u5.s4.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u5.s4.f1: Payout ratio = dividend per share ÷ earnings per share; total return ≈ price return + dividend return
lesson.u5.s4.f1note: A higher payout ratio leaves less profit inside the company for reinvestment.
lesson.u5.s4.p1: Total return has two parts: price change (price return) and dividends (income return). Looking only at the share price ignores cash payouts.
lesson.u5.s4.p2: Reinvesting dividends buys more shares, which increases the base for future dividends and compounds over time, but the result still depends on the share price.
lesson.u5.s4.pro.text: Sustainable dividends usually come from stable free cash flow. A high payout ratio can limit reinvestment or force a cut when earnings fall.

lesson.u5.s4.title: Dividend reinvestment and total return
lesson.u5.s4.warn.text: Dividend reinvestment is not risk-free compounding: prices can fall and payouts can be cut. A historical yield is not a promise.

lesson.u6.s1.example.l1: Two companies both earn $1 per share. The market pays 40× earnings for the growth stock, about $40, and 15× for the mature company, about $15.
lesson.u6.s1.example.l2: The extra you pay for the growth stock buys future growth expectations, not current earnings.
lesson.u6.s1.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u6.s1.p1: Growth stocks grow revenue and earnings faster than the market average. They usually reinvest most profits into research, expansion or acquisitions, so dividends are small or zero.
lesson.u6.s1.p2: The market pays a higher valuation for sustained growth. If growth slows or expectations miss, both the valuation and the share price can fall, so growth stocks are often more volatile.
lesson.u6.s1.title: Growth stocks: paying for growth
lesson.u6.s1.warn.text: High valuations must be justified by sustained growth. If growth disappoints, the share price can fall sharply.

lesson.u6.s2.p1: Value stocks trade low relative to earnings, assets or cash flow. They may be undervalued, or cheap because fundamentals are deteriorating; cheap alone is not a reason to buy.
lesson.u6.s2.p2: Cyclical stocks have profits that swing with the economy, common in industrials, materials, energy and discretionary consumer sectors. Earnings can be strong in expansions and fall quickly in recessions.
lesson.u6.s2.pro.text: Style labels are not permanent. Companies grow, mature or decline; classification is a starting point, not a substitute for fundamental research.

lesson.u6.s3.myth.text: "Value stocks are always safe and growth stocks always make money" are both false. Style describes characteristics, not guaranteed returns.
lesson.u6.s3.myth.title: Common myth
lesson.u6.s3.p1: Income companies are usually mature with stable cash flow, distributing a larger share of profits as dividends, but with limited growth.
lesson.u6.s3.p2: Do not rely on the label alone. A high yield can come from a falling price; a growth stock may start paying dividends; a cyclical stock can look cheap at a cycle peak.

lesson.u7.s1.list.title: Common ETF types
lesson.u7.s1.p1: An ETF is a basket of assets traded on an exchange, with a ticker and a quote like a stock. It usually tracks an index, sector or theme.
lesson.u7.s1.p2: Buying one ETF share gives indirect exposure to all its components, so it is diversified by construction. Costs are usually below active funds, but management fees and spreads still apply.
lesson.u7.s1.title: ETFs: one ticker, a basket of assets
lesson.u7.s1.warn.text: Diversification is not the absence of risk. Sector ETFs can be highly concentrated, and broad ETFs still fall with the overall market. Completing Unit 7 unlocks five tradable ETFs with live quotes that can be bought, sold and shorted like stocks.
lesson.u7.s1.warn.title: Risk note
lesson.u7.s2.example.l1: A single stock has 30% annualised volatility; spreading money equally across three companies in different sectors may produce lower portfolio volatility.
lesson.u7.s2.example.l2: If all three are in the same sector and fall together, the diversification benefit is much smaller.
lesson.u7.s2.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u7.s2.p1: Diversification spreads money across different assets to reduce company- or sector-specific risk. It cannot remove overall market risk.
lesson.u7.s2.p2: The benefit depends on correlation: assets that always move together provide little diversification, while low-correlation assets usually produce a smoother portfolio.

lesson.u7.s3.example.l2: If one position grows to $4,000, rebalancing sells about $333 and adds it to the other two.

lesson.u7.s3.p1: You can build your own ETF with 3–5 stocks from different sectors, bought at target weights.
lesson.u7.s3.p2: Prices move and weights drift. Rebalancing sells what has grown and buys what has shrunk to restore the target weights and control risk.
lesson.u7.s3.pro.text: Rebalancing costs commissions and can reduce short-term returns; its main purpose is controlling risk exposure, not guaranteeing a higher return.

lesson.u8.s1.f1note: This assumes annual compounding and a constant return with all interest reinvested.
lesson.u8.s1.p1: Simple interest is paid only on the original principal. Compound interest adds each period's interest to the principal so that future interest is earned on it too.
lesson.u8.s1.p2: Compounding depends on time and reinvestment. With the same annual return, starting earlier produces faster growth later.
lesson.u8.s1.title: Simple versus compound interest
lesson.u8.s2.example.l1: $1,000 initial plus $100 a month at 7% for 20 years ends near $56,000.
lesson.u8.s2.example.l2: About $25,000 comes from contributions and the rest from compounding; change the demo parameters to verify.

lesson.u8.s2.p1: Regular contributions amplify compounding because every new deposit also earns future returns.
lesson.u8.s2.p2: Compounding is very sensitive to return. 7% versus 10% over 30 years is a huge difference, but higher assumed returns usually mean higher risk.
lesson.u8.s2.pro.text: Nominal returns must cover fees and inflation. Real purchasing power growth can be much lower than the headline number.

lesson.u8.s3.p1: Long-term investing is not set-and-forget. You still need to control concentration, fees and risk, and revisit your assumptions.
lesson.u8.s3.p2: Drawdowns are asymmetric: a 50% fall requires a 100% gain to recover, and a large drawdown significantly slows the compounding curve.

lesson.u9.s1.p1: A candlestick records the open, high, low and close for one period. This game uses daily candles, so each candle is one trading session.
lesson.u9.s1.p2: The body spans open to close. The upper wick reaches the high and the lower wick reaches the low. A close above the open is a bullish (green) candle; a close below the open is bearish (red).

lesson.u9.s2.warn.text: One candle cannot predict the future. The same shape means something different in an uptrend, a downtrend or a range.

lesson.u9.s3.example.l1: A long upper wick at the end of an uptrend can signal stronger selling pressure.
lesson.u9.s3.example.l2: A long lower wick in a downtrend can show buying support, or simply a brief bounce.
lesson.u9.s3.example.title: Worked example
lesson.u9.s3.p1: A long upper wick shows a rally that faded; a long lower wick shows a dip that recovered; a doji means open and close were close together.
lesson.u9.s3.p2: Shapes are traces of supply and demand, not guaranteed signals. Read them together with trend, volume and news context.

quant.ml.configSubtitle: A cross-sectional market model that never changes the simulated account.
quant.ml.disclaimer: The model uses price-derived factors only and a limited sample; accuracy and past returns are not forecasts.
quant.ml.modelNote: Features are standardised per cross-section; logistic regression shows weights and neural models show hidden-layer feature importance. News sentiment uses a 20-day window.
quant.ml.overfitClear: Out-of-sample results look acceptable, but more data and cost assumptions are still needed.
quant.ml.overfitWarning: Out-of-sample accuracy or returns are weak; the model may be overfit. Do not use it for real trading.
quant.ml.tuningNote: Auto tuning carves a validation slice out of the training set; the out-of-sample test is never used for selection.
quant.mode.backtestDesc: Run one strategy on the full sample and inspect metrics and trades.
quant.mode.mlDesc: Train cross-sectional models on momentum, low-vol, trend, news sentiment, sentiment change, analyst revisions, volume and money-flow factors, optionally search network architectures, then test an out-of-sample stock portfolio.
quant.mode.optimizeDesc: Search a parameter grid for the best in-sample result, then test it out of sample for overfitting.
quant.mode.regressionDesc: Estimate factor premia, Rank IC and explanatory power (R²) with a pooled cross-sectional regression.
quant.note: The backtest only uses completed daily bars, generates signals at the close and fills at the next open. Results are for teaching and falsification, not forecasts.
quant.opt.bestNote: Parameters are chosen in-sample only; out-of-sample results never influence the search.
quant.opt.bestSubtitle: Ranked by the objective inside the training sample
quant.opt.chartNote: The OOS curve checks robustness and never participates in parameter selection.
quant.opt.chartTitle: Out-of-sample equity of the best parameters
quant.opt.disclaimer: Grid search itself raises the chance of overfitting; OOS results describe this sample only and do not guarantee future performance.
quant.opt.gridNote: The optimiser searches the built-in grid and picks the best in-sample set for the chosen objective; focus on the OOS result.
quant.opt.overfitClear: Out-of-sample performance did not collapse, but it still describes only this history.
quant.opt.overfitWarning: Out-of-sample performance is much weaker; this parameter set may be overfit. Do not deploy it directly.
quant.reg.configSubtitle: Pooled cross-sectional regression; research only, the simulated account is unchanged.
quant.reg.disclaimer: The regression only describes average in-sample relationships; factor premia change with the market regime and are not forecasts.
quant.reg.note: Runs a pooled OLS with an intercept on each day's factor cross-section and forward returns; features are standardised per date, so a coefficient is the average return tied to a one-standard-deviation move.
quant.reg.tableSubtitle: Coefficients are average returns (%); IC is the mean cross-sectional Rank IC

quiz.u6.q1.o2: It pays a high fixed dividend

roadmap.note: The roadmap may change. This project deliberately uses fictional companies and deterministic simulated quotes only: it does not connect to live market data and does not file real taxes. Shipped features include options, short selling, margin, futures, career progression, fund management, the Quant Lab, Macro World, bonds / FX / commodities / crypto and the simulated exchange; exchange challenge modes, time-travel review, advanced orders and physical option settlement are complete; options support European / American styles, with deterministic early assignment for deep in-the-money short legs.

settings.scope.p1j: Multi-asset: bond coupon present-value pricing and yield marking, USD-quoted FX, commodity pricing and fractional crypto trading with unified daily revaluation
settings.scope.p1k: Intraday data: simulated candles per tick, a daily/intraday chart switch and an optional external JSON live-quote channel with CORS, refresh interval and source labels
